speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MOTION FOR SITTINGS FROM 2 TO 6 AND FROM 7 TO 11 P.M.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that I invited my friends the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties to meet with me yesterday afternoon at five o'clock to see if we could not together work out a plan that might help to expedite the business of the session. I am happy to say that all were agreed that if hon. members would lend their support it would be advisable to have the house meet from two o'clock until six and from seven until eleven each day from tomorrow until the end of the session. There was some consideration of the question of beginning morning sittings, but it was thought that at least for the present hon. members would prefer to meet for a longer number of hours in the afternoon and evening and have the morning free. If we are hard pressed to get through at the time we hope it may be possible to get through, we shall consider the possibility of meeting on Saturdays as well.
I may say that this plan has back of it the hope and, possibly, the expectation that if all hon. members cooperate we might be able to wind up the business of the house towards the end of the first week of July. That will depend altogether on cooperation between the different parties and the support of their members in the house. To that end we have considered what were the most important measures still on the order paper and the general wish that they should be brought forward as soon as possible. My colleague, the house leader, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) announced last night that there would be two important measures proceeded with today, the resolution of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) respecting industrial relations and investigation of industrial disputes, and the resolution to amend the Old Age Pensions Act. How far we can proceed with these measures will depend upon the general consent the house may be prepared to give.
It was thought it would best suit the convenience of hon. members and help to expedite business if we reserved Wednesday evenings and all day on Fridays for the consideration of estimates. By knowing in advance that no government measures other than supply would be taken up on Wednesday evenings and on Fridays hon. members would be in a better position so to arrange their time as to give it to those matters in which they are most interested. On Mondays, it was felt we might take up any measures that are on the order paper. It would not however be the purpose of the government to bring forward on Mondays the most important measures.
I think that covers pretty much the line of agreement that we reached in the course of our conference.
There is a small bill which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is interested in bringing before the house as soon as possible, an act to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932, notice of which appears in the Votes and Proceedings. In order to have it presented to the house today the house would have to give its unanimous consent. If that
House of Commons

can be given the Minister of Finance will introduce that bill first thing this afternoon.
With respect to some of the measures I have mentioned there was also the feeling that if we could have it generally agreed that the discussion would take place on the bills rather than on the resolutions that would greatly expedite the business.
There appears in the Votes and Proceedings of today, Mr. Speaker, a motion that the house meet tomorrow at two o'clock and from then on until the end of the session along the lines I have indicated. As the notice of motion appears there is some lack of punctuation or a small hiatus in printing that might mislead the members, but I will read the motion as it would appear if correctly punctuated and will ask that it be presented to the house immediately. Under the rules of the house this motion does not require any notice:
That on and after Wednesday, June 18 instant, until the end of the session, the house shall meet at two o'clock p.m. of each sitting day; and at six o'clock p.m., Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair until seven o'clock, all notwithstanding any standing order or resolution of the house in relation thereto.

subtopic: AIR MAIL TO TELECRAPH CREEK, B.C.
speechtext: On the 4th of June the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) inquired respecting delay in the delivery of mail for Telegraph Creek, B.C. I took the question as a notice, and the answer is as follows: I have now established that the difficulty in this case arose from the change-over from winter to summer routing of mail for Telegraph Creek. In the winter, mail for that post office is dispatched from Vancouver to Carcross, Yukon, whence it is forwarded by air stage service to destination. In the summer the mail is dispatched to Wrangell, Alaska, whence it is forwarded by river boat to Telegraph Creek. The last air stage flight from Car-cross to Telegraph Creek for the winter season was made on April 2, and mail dispatched to Carcross on April 8 and 19 had to be reforwarded from the latter point to Wrangell to connect with the river boat to Telegraph Creek. Since April 30, mail for Telegraph Creek has been regularly forwarded via Wrangell.

Industrial Disputes

INVESTIGATION, CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT *-PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC.
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
_ That it is expedient to present a bill respecting industrial relations and investigation of industrial disputes and to make provision therein for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the remuneration and expenses of the members of the boards and commissions and the officers, clerks and employees appointed or engaged by or under the authority of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

This bill is intended to replace the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, chapter 112, revised statutes of Canada. 1927, which had been the main federal labour law from 1907 until February, 1944, when by order in council we suspended the operation of the act and gave effect to P.C. 1003, commonly known as the wartime labour relations regulations.
Last year we had a conference with ministers of labour of the various provinces and their officials, at which we discussed the more important principles of a new federal law- and, I may add, in a very encouraging atmosphere of cooperation.
The chief purpose of the conference, of course, was to obtain the views of the provinces as to when it would be most appropriate to restore to the provinces full responsibility for dealing with industrial disputes in industries ordinarily under their jurisdiction.
As hon. members know, the provinces resumed their full jurisdiction in these matters, some on March 31 and others on May 15. The bill now before the house applies only to employees and employers in industries under the jurisdiction of parliament, as follows:
(a)	Works, undertakings or businesses operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada;
(b)	Railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting a province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of a province;
(c)	Lines of steam and other ships connecting a province with any other or others of the provinces or extending beyond the limits of a province;

(d)	Ferries between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada;
(e)	Aerodromes, aircraft and lines of air transportation;
(f)	Radio broadcasting stations;
(g)	Such works or undertakings as, although wholly situate within a province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces; and
(h)	Any work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislature of any province.
The act will apply also to crown corporations unless excluded by the governor in council.
P.C. 1003 was found to be of great value in contributing to stable labour relations during the critical war years and since, and we have included in the new legislation the best features of that order, changed in some respects and amplified in others, based upon the experience gained in its administration. We have also taken into consideration more recent representations which have been made to us by the provinces and by labour and employer organizations.
I believe the committee will agree with me that it is most important we should have an act for the settlement of industrial disputes which will be fair to the worker and employer alike and that will make possible the equitable and sensible adjustment of differences between them.
The legislation provides what I consider are appropriate procedures and conciliation machinery to deal with disputes of this character affecting undertakings over which parliament has legislative authority. It establishes procedures for the negotiation of collective agreements on wages and other terms of employment, giving the employees the right to organize for the purpose of collective bargaining without interference and to be represented in negotiations by a trade union of their own choice.
In disputes arising out of the negotiation of collective agreements, strikes and lockouts and the taking of strike votes among employees are prohibited until the procedures of negotiation and conciliation laid down in the act have been completely followed. Strikes and lockouts also are prohibited during the time that a collective agreement is in effect, except where the parties have agreed to renegotiate a provision of the agreement before the whole agreement terminates. In any

Industrial Disputes
case of renegotiation the provisions for such conciliation which I have mentioned would apply.
The provisions of part I of the act are capable of being applied, by provincial legislation, to all or any particular industry within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
In other words, we have tried to set a pattern which some of the provinces may care to apply knowing that we shall not be moving as rapidly as we should towards the goal of industrial peace in this country if we have widely varying legislation of this nature in the spheres of dominion and provincial operation.
The unfair labour practices section of the act will prohibit discrimination by employers against employees on account of trade union membership or activity or interference by them in the organization and carrying on of a trade union. Likewise it will be unlawful for any person to use coercion to compel anyone to become, or not to become, a member of a trade union. Trade union organizing work in a plant during working hours is prohibited except with the consent of the employer.
The question of certification of a trade union is, of course, important, and the act provides that a union may obtain recognition as the exclusive bargaining agent of employees if it satisfies the labour relations board that its membership represents a majority of the employees in the bargaining unit which the board also has the authority to define.
The board may order a secret vote where it is considered necessary. In order to take care of a jurisdictional dispute between unions, provision is made for a new certification to be granted if application is made after the expiry of ten months of the term of a collective agreement.
An employees' organization dominated by an employer is not recognized under the act, and there also is a provision revoking the authority of a union to serve as the exclusive bargaining agent when it is shown that the union has lost the support of the majority of the employees.
Once a union has been certified as a bargaining agent, the parties are required to enter into negotiations for the conclusion of a collective agreement. If they cannot settle matters between themselves, then the act requires them to obtain the conciliation services of the Department of Labour. If that fails, a conciliation board may be appointed by the Minister of Labour upon the request of either party. This applies to the renegotiation of existing agreements.
An important provision of the act prohibits an employer declaring a lockout, employees
going on strike, the taking of a strike vote or the declaration of a strike until all conciliation procedures have been exhausted and fourteen days have elapsed.
Parties negotiating a collective agreement are required to include in the agreement an appropriate provision for final settlement by arbitration or otherwise, without stoppage of work, of disputes which arise between the employees who are bound by the agreement and their employer during the currency of the agreement, concerning the meaning or violation of the agreement. Where an agreement does not contain such provision, the labour relations board is authorized to write it into the agreement.
A further provision of the act authorizes the appointment by the Minister of Labour of an industrial disputes inquiry commission of one or more persons for the purpose of looking into any industrial dispute and to report thereon. This provision is similar to the provisions of P.C. 4020, an order in council which was extensively used during the war.
For administrative purposes, it is proposed that we establish what will be known as the Canada labour relations board, to be composed of a chairman and not more than eight other members equally representative of labour and employers.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we have received representations for the inclusion of measures severely curtailing union activities; from others have come suggestions which would involve, under certain conditions, the compulsory application of the principle of union security in collective agreements and the adoption of other innovations.
We have not given effect in this legislation to such representations, since it is not the desire of the government to place impediments in the way of free collective bargaining between employers and their organized workers, or to legislate conditions or terms of employment that properly lie in the field of collective bargaining.
The essential purpose of the legislation is to create conditions favourable to the free exercise of the collective bargaining function in order that negotiations between the parties to a dispute can be carried on with the greatest degree of success.
For that reason, only such regulation of employer and employee activity in their industrial relationships considered as necessary to protect the public interest is incorporated in the legislation. It leaves with labour and management the major responsibility of settling between them their problems in regard to negotiation of collective
Industrial Disputes

agreements and administration of such agreements.
It has long been my view that legislation of this nature will fail in its fundamental objective if it introduces features of a punitive and coercive character which could only result in driving employers and employees further apart. That would make it more difficult for them to establish those friendly relations of good will and cooperation which are so necessary.
Human nature cannot be corrected by a law, and in the final analysis, Mr. Chairman, the major consideration in improving human relations between employers and employees is the simple matter of trying to see each other's point of view and developing mutual understanding.

I should like to ask the
minister one or two questions, the answers to which I think it is only proper that the committee should have, with regard to the legislation now before us. The act used to be called the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act; it is now changed by having the word "relations" added to it. It is to be called the Industrial Relations and Investigation of Industrial Disputes Act. So far, so good. But does this statute apply to public utilities? Some of the utilities are publicly-owned, such as those having to do with light, power and transportation. For instance, there are the street railways. A strike may occur next winter, for one of many reasons, in the light or power services shutting off power or light at a time when meals are being prepared. In view of the decision of the privy council in the Snider case, it is doubtful whether the dominion has jurisdiction over some classes of public utilities such as those having to do with power. If we are to make any change in the remuneration of these boards, we should have value for the money expended. In view of the difficulties we have had during the war and after, may I ask if the act will be made effective by any change of name? Is it a mandatory act? Does it compel the two sides to come together? Why should the citizens of the city of Ottawa or of any other city suffer because of a strike brought against the public? In view of the changes now made in the act, and of the wide discussions in Washington on the subject, are we getting some proper method of bringing the parties together, which we should have, when the law is brought into force?

I can answer my hon. friend in two minutes. I think I have a recollection of what he called the Snider case. That was some twenty years ago. The industries referred to by my hon. friend of course come purely within provincial jurisdiction.

I understand that any general debate in this matter is to take place on second reading; in that I most heartily concur. Speaking for most of the party over here, I wish to say that we will not debate the matter now, but will reserve our rights until the bill comes up for second reading.

I cannot permit a debate between the hon. gentleman and the minister at this stage. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	What the right hon. Secretary of
State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) has said is perfectly right. We can send this bill to the committee on external affairs or any other committee only after it is given-second reading. Then if it is reported by the committee it may come before the committee of the whole house, as the minister said would be done. On the other hand the right hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) expressed a wrong view when he said the giving of second reading would not be an acceptance of the principle of the bill. I remember very well what happened in regard to the precedent the minister quoted, the Bank of Canada Act. The parties were unanimous in accepting the principle of that bill, because it was one of the fourteen points of the Liberal party which Mr. Bennett had stolen. So there was no disagreement as to the principle, which was admitted by the whole house.
Here the question is obvious. This is one case where we will have to decide whether we shall have world government or keep the constitution of this country. That and nothing else is the obvious question. It is part of the scheme to bring Canada under the dominion and jurisdiction of a world government. Where it will stop I do not know. This is a theory which has been expressed by some leading men of the world, that we should be governed by a super-administration belonging to all the big powers. I am opposed to that, in the first place because I do not believe that the right of justice belongs to the so-called big powers. That is the first thing. In the second place I do not believe the big powers have been so successful or have shown such good results in what they have done up to the present. In the third place, if things go on like this I am afraid this country will be the trailer of alii the other countries of the world, and we in this parliament will be just rubber stamps.
If we are to keep the constitution as it is we cannot accept this kind of government. I am very sorry to have to rise and express personal views about this matter, but they come from deep convictions. If I had not a deep conviction, the constitution being what it is and what it has been for eighty years,
I would leave it at that, close my eyes and let it pass.
I do not want to detain the house by making a long speech. If human rights exist, if we in this house intend to apply them to all other nations, then we cannot forget that one of those rights is freedom of speech. Shall we

United Nations
still have that right with an organization like that? They do not have freedom of speech in Russia; they hardly have freedom of speech in France, and they do not have it in China. They still have it in the United States, as in England, but we know nothing about the future. I say all this with the most friendly disposition.
Do hon. members realize the immunities that are to be given to the representatives of all the specialized agencies of the united nations? The list is formidable; it is enormous. The other day I asked for that information, and the right hon. minister who is sponsoring the bill was kind enough to give me a copy of it. Here they are:
Representatives of members to the principal and subsidiary organs-
Not only the principal, but also the subsidiary organs.
-of the united nations and to conferences convened by the united nations, shall, while exercising their functions and during their journey to and from the place of meeting, enjoy the following privileges and immunities:
(a)	immunity from personal arrest or detention and from seizure of their personal baggage, and, in respect of words spoken or written and all acts done by them in their capacity as representatives. immunity from legal process of every kind;
(b)	inviolability for all papers and documents ;
(c)	the right to use codes and to receive papers or correspondence 'by courier or in sealed bags;
(d)	exemption in respect of themselves and their spouses from immigration restrictions, aliens registration or national service obligations in the state they are visiting or through which they are passing in the exercise of their functions;
(e)	the same facilities in respect of currency or exchange restrictions as are accorded to representatives of foreign governments on temporary official missions;
(f)	the same immunities and facilities in respect of their personal baggage as are accorded to diplomatic envoys; and also,
(g)	such other privileges, immunities and facilities not inconsistent with the foregoing as diplomatic envoys enjoy, except that they shall have no right to claim exemption from customs duties on goods imported (otherwise than as part of their personal baggage) or from excise duties or sales taxes.
They can bring in as many trunks as they wish without paying any duty. When they are in the country they cannot import goods from their own or other countries free of customs duties, but that is the only difference from fully accredited diplomats. That is going pretty far. My deep regret is that the united nations are following the same lines as the old defunct league of nations. No imagination is being shown, and we are much worse off than before because all these people who belong, not only to the specialized agencies
but to their subsidiaries, will have the same rights as ministers and ambassadors.
Quite often I express personal views, but they are sincere. Sometimes I have the support of hon. members of my party; sometimes I have the support of all groups of the opposition, but in this case I want to congratulate publicly the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) upon the foresight they showed when we were in the resolution stage. We may differ at times, but opinions are free. The hon. gentlemen to whom I have just referred meant what they said, as I did. We were sincere in this matter. We gave a solemn warning to the government not to be caught in the web of the united nations.
I entertain great fears about these people, for the reasons that I have given. I do not trust most of them. Nobody trusts them individually, but when it comes to considering them jointly we are all ready to accept anything from them. How is it that when we will not accept the form of super-government they have, we are ready to accept orders and instructions given by those governments? We may trust a few of these governments, but we do not trust all of them. The majority of the big powers have governments that we would not accept. We would not accept the government of Russia, the government of China or the present unstable government of France. With regard to the socialistic government of England and the capitalistic government of the United States, there are differences of opinion. In the case of three out of five they have governments which we would not accept in this country. I challenge any group to say that they would accept any of those three governments. Yet they represent a majority in the government of the united nations. Small nations like Canada will have no say.
We will see caravans of members of specialized agencies and their subsidiaries crossing Canada and living here, and they will be quite free as long as they can show credentials given by any country. The deep fear I have is that it will encourage spying. Their belongings will be untouchable, and it will be impossible to verify what papers they may have because they will be under diplomatic seal just the same as those of ambassadors, ministers and high commissioners. They will be given special privileges, and I am against special privileges. It is all right to receive the representatives of foreign countries, but what about international organizations that are most dangerous? The control of those organizations, and even the control of the united
United, Nations

nations, may be taken over by one of the three dangerous governments I have mentioned.
I want to make myself clear: I do not condemn the people of the big five countries, but I entertain fears about their governments. I would remind the house that the song of Soviet Russia is "The Internationale". The idea of Russia is to create that kind of feeling which will destroy patriotism in all other nations. Then when there is no more patriotism we shall have an international organization where right counts no longer and where might is always right. Those powers will try in their own way to take control of the united nations and establish communism throughout the world. Canada does not count before the united nations. It may count socially but not politically.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to establish a corporation to be known as the dominion coal board to administer subventions or subsidies relating to coal voted by parliament, to exercise and perform certain other powers, duties and functions.
Provision is made further for the advisory functions of the board, for the employment of professional and technical advisers and assistants and their remuneration, and for all expenses of the act to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement on this resolution?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Yes. This resolution provides for the establishment of a dominion coal board as a further step towards solving a problem that has been before this house and the people of Canada for the past seventy years. The first report on coal which has come to my notice is by a select committee of the House of Commons, dated April 27, 1877, dealing with "the state of the coal trade and for the promoting of interprovincial trade". That report suggested that bounties and subsidies be granted for the movement of Nova Scotia coal to points in Quebec and Ontario.
The intervening years have produced numerous reports on coal by parliamentary committees, royal commissions, and provincial commissions. The last report on the subject is entitled "Report of the Royal Commission on Coal", which was tabled in this house on January 31, 1947. The report represents months of careful and conscientious study by the commissioners, and I commend it to all members of this house for careful study.
Direct intervention by the government in the production and distribution of coal dates
	'
back to June, 1917, when the government appointed a coal controller to deal with fuel difficulties that were an outgrowth of the war period. At that time it became necessary to make regulations to protect the production, sale, delivery and consumption of all fuels to meet wartime requirements. The final report of the first coal controller, dated March, 1919, stressed the necessity for having a continuing body to deal with coal supplies generally. The dominion fuel board was created by order in council in November, 1922, and since that time has functioned within its original terms of reference. The recent royal commission report states that the powers of the present board are not sufficiently wide in scope to deal with the present problem.
Shortly after the outbreak of the second world war, the government appointed a coal administrator under the wartime prices and trade board, with jurisdiction over the supply, distribution and price of coal. The staff of the dominion fuel board was taken over by the coal administrator. By 1942 the problem of coal supply became of paramount importance and to deal with it the government appointed an emergency coal production board under the chairmanship of the coal administrator. Shortly after this, since supply problems generally were being dealt with by the Departs ment of Munitions and Supply, the duties and responsibilities of the coal administrator were transferred to that department under the direction of a coal controller.
Coal control ended on December 31, 1946, and the functions of coal administration ended with the lifting of the price ceiling on coal on April 15, 1947. At that time, the dominion fuel board was reconstituted and is at present functioning within its original terms of reference.
The government is in full agreement with the recommendation of the royal commission on coal that a dominion coal board be established and charged with the responsibility for implementing the recommendations of the report. The board will take over the records of the dominion fuel board, as well as those of wartime controls, and these will form a valuable background for the work of the new board. I might add that, if proof is needed that these records are valuable, it will be found in the fact that during the period of wartime coal control it was possible to arrange for supplies of coal that maintained full industrial production without one day's loss of time from coal shortage, as well as a full supply to the household consumer.
Much has been said and written about the Canadian coal problem. This is not a single problem-we have many coal problems, differ-

Dominion Coal Board
ing in kind and degree. There is the problem of maintaining an adequate supply of coal for our national requirements, and there is also the problem of building up in Canada a sound and healthy producing industry. There is the problem of finding steady and adequate markets for Canadian coal, and the problem of providing reasonably full employment at fair wages for our miners. Each section of Canada has its own coal problem, differing from that of other sections.
The report of the royal commission on coal accepts the necessity for industries in central Canada to secure the major portion of their coal requirements from the United States. Developments in low cost production and transportation may possibly alter this concept in some measure in the future, but it would appear that for many years industry and households in central Ontario will continue to secure supplies from the nearest source, namely, the immense deposits in the Appalachian field in the United States. However, this finding need not preclude the growing development of a stable and prosperous producing industry within this country; nor need it preclude the provision of an increasing and remunerative field of employment for Canadian coal miners.
The commission has found that the government policy of subventions to assist transportation of coal, arising out of investigations made by a special committee of the House of Commons in 1921, has been both well designed and reasonably adequate, and should be continued. This subvention policy has been directed primarily to the marketing phase of the Canadian coal industry. The problem of providing and maintaining an adequate market for Canadian coal is constantly changing, and does not, by its very nature, lend itself to the establishment of a rigid and invarying policy. Therefore the commission recommends that the present dominion fuel board, composed of civil servants, be replaced by a new statutory body which will serve full time in the administration of present subvention policies and such new measures of assistance as may be required from time to time. In this way the marketing problem will receive the constant attention of a body set up for the purpose. The resolution now under discussion has for its purpose the implementation of this recommendation.
I will now discuss the other main problem, namely, the production of coal throughout Canada at the lowest possible cost. The report of the commission gives the salient features of the operations in each of Canada's main coal fields. In normal times, and during 83166-271J
the war, the industry has been in a healthy state in Saskatchewan, and in Alberta, including the southeast corner of British Columbia. On the other hand operations on Vancouver island, and particularly in the maritine provinces, have not been in a healthy condition for many years. The mines producing industrial and railway coal in the mountain regions in British Columbia have had a particularly good record. The profits of the group are not excessive, but in wages paid, in constant and increasing output, and in efficiency of production, these operations stand out over the general average. The production of domestic coal in Alberta has suffered from seasonal operation, inherent in the nature of the coal, but even under this handicap shows a sound and encouraging record. The lignite coal mines in Saskatchewan have built up by their own efforts a sound and profitable market, and have a record of expansion that is by no means ended. There are few serious problems in the operation of this section of the industry that cannot be solved by the industry itself. The provision of a stable market for the industrial and railway coals is bound up with the general prosperity of the country, but there would appear to be good prospects for the maintenance of an adequate and orderly marketing of the output from this area. The greatest improvement can be effected by developments in research that will solve the present seasonal fluctuations in the production of domestic coal in both Alberta and Saskatchewan. When the solution for this problem can foe found, the freight subvention policy recommended in the commission's report should be adeqaute for this section of the industry.
The coal fields of Vancouver island represent a special problem. The output per man day has been consistently lower than in the mountain and prairie mines, and the market has been restricted and highly competitive as against other fuels, such as oil and wood. For the past four or five years there has been a market for every ton of coal that could be produced, but for a variety of reasons, the mines have not increased their output to meet the challenge. In fact production has gone down, and it has been necessary to sustain operations by means of production subsidies. The ending of production subsidies calls for a reorganized production programme, required to maintain a sound and healthy coal producing industry on Vancouver island.
A still more serious outlook is presented by present conditions in the maritime provinces, and particularly in the Cape Breton area. We have here the largest concentration of the Canadian coal mining industry, located
Dominion Coal Board

in a heavily populated area, that is almost wholly dependent on this industry for means of livelihood. The other large maritime industry, steel, depends for its wellbeing upon an adequate supply of coal, at a cost that will permit the sale of its products at competitive prices. Maximum production from the maritime coal fields has been a matter of national necessity during the two great wars within our generation. Thus the maritime coal problem is of the highest importance, not only to that locality but to all parts of Canada.
Mining has been carried on continuously in the Cape Breton field for a longer period than in any other Canadian area, and part of the problem arises from the technical difficulties,, inherent both in the nature of the deposits, and in the very fact that mining operations have continued along lines laid down years ago. The methods adapted to mining of coal in earlier years may not be best adapted to the present situation. The royal commission report devotes considerable space to mining methods in these areas.
The production of coal in the maritime provinces, since early in the war, has presented an increasingly difficult and distressing problem. Production in this area has dropped by over two million tons per annum from normal, and the cost of production has skyrocketed to the point that the federal government has been obliged to provide upwards of twenty million dollars to the mine owners since January 1, 1942, in production subsidies, to prevent the industry from collapsing. The operators have placed the blame for decreased efficiency and higher cost on labour, and in turn, labour has been very critical of the management.
Special production subsidies no longer can be justified. The royal commission recommends the ending of production subsidies, but two of the commissioners suggest continued government aid to the maritime industry for a short reconversion period. The report is definite in its indication that the industry must expect to stand on its own feet, except for enlargements of its markets through freight subventions. Unless increased production' can be obtained, subvention assistance is likely to be of little benefit, as production of coal, and its consumption, are at present about in balance within maritime provinces.
In pre-war years, wages for coal miners in the maritime provinces have been lower than in other fields, and the necessity for this disparity was recognized and accepted. It is, however, an unsound policy to attempt to Derpetuate an industry through low wages.

Therefore every effort must be exerted to provide,. through a return to low cost and efficient production, for the payment of wages that will return a fair and reasonable standard of living to the workers. We are faced with the outstanding fact that if production in [DOT] the mines were brought up only as far as the pre-war level of efficiency, the present difficulty would fade and disappear. Such an improvement would provide for increases in wage scale, as well as for surplus earnings available to management for necessaiy mine improvements.
I would sum up the maritime situation by saying that unless the problems facing, the industry are quickly solved, the industry is heading for disaster. The problem of restoring the coal industry of the maritime provinces to a healthy condition is wrapped up with the continued prosperity of the area, and constitutes a plain challenge to private enterprise, as it is also a challenge to organized labour.
The coal report concludes with both majority and minority recommendations, but it is interesting to note that there is in fact a substantial measure of unanimity. There is agreement with the policy of assisting Canadian coal to find a wider market by means of subventions and the present tariff, as that policy has been developed and administered in the past, is sound and should be continued, although there are some small differences of opinion as to the future scope of the policy. The commissioners are unanimous in the opinion that nationalization of the industry, in whole or in part, does not offer any promise of improvement over present conditions. There is agreement that a statutory board should be established to carry on the functions of the dominion fuel board and to assume additional responsibilities in the national interest.
Returning to the supply problem in Ontario and Quebec, geography and economics make it inevitable that these provinces must depend largely on imported coal. Thus the supply is subject to interruptions beyond the control of Canada. We had an example last summer, when you will recall that a protracted coal strike in the United States was followed by a protracted seaman's strike in Canada. Strikes in the steel industry in the United States, result was that at September 1 our imports were three and one-half million tons lower for that period than would supply our minimum requirements. I had every reason to fear that Canada would face a situation this winter similar to last winter's situation in the United Kingdom. However, the coal controller and his staff combined with the Canadian shipping board, both of which had war emergency powers, in a determined effort to correct the situation. Lake carriers

Dominion Coal Board
were taken out of their normal trades and diverted to the carriage of coal. Emergency arrangements were made to transport Alberta coal to Ontario markets and to move American coal by rail into this area. The result was that the close of navigation found us with our minimum requirements provided for, plus one and one-half million tons of bituminous coal, and one million tons of anthracite coal, as an additional cushion against further interruptions to supply. This correction could not have been made without the agency of overriding emergency powers. If in future Ontario and Quebec are to have reasonable security of coal supply, it seems necessary that the new statutory board must be clothed with emergency powers adequate to enable that board to deal quickly with any dangerous situation that may arise. The bill based on this resolution will provide accordingly.
Hon. members will find in the resolution and in the bill to come before them, the details of the constitution, responsibilities and authority of the proposed new board. These have been drafted in general accordance with the recommendations of the royal commission, and it has been considered advisable to avoid any attempt to circumscribe the usefulness of this new body by too precise a definition. In the last analysis the responsibility for policy must rest directly upon parliament and government, since the expenditure of public funds will be directly concerned. The matters with which the board will deal are, however, so diverse in character that it will be necessary, for the efficient discharge of the responsibilities imposed, that a wide area of authority be provided for investigation and consideration. The implementation of the findings of the new body will remain the responsibility of government.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF SUBVENTIONS OR SUBSIDIES VOTED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The report of the royal commission on coal has been in our hands for some time. This resolution provides first:
That it is expedient to present a bill to establish a corporation-
In the first place, the minister has given us no reason why this should be a corporation. It is just one of the many crown corporations which we have been forming in times gone by, although in this particular case I can see no reason whatever for clothing this arm of government with corporate powers and then taking it, like other things, outside the civil service, outside audit by the auditor general, and so on. The minister did not mention that in his statement. There may be a reason, but if there is it is quite unknown to me. The resolution continues:
-to be known as the dominion coal board to administer subventions or subsidies relating to coal voted by parliament, to exercise and perform certain other powers, duties and functions.
The last remark the minister made was, I think, the only one he made with respect to these other powers, duties and functions, when he said that he intended to clothe this board with emergency powers. The recommendations of the royal commission are found on two pages, 582-3, of their report, and Mr. Justice Carroll and Mr. Justice McLaurin had this to say. The last paragraph is really the acting one:
It is not generally practical to fix subvention aid by statute because the assistance must vary from time to time with changes in the competitive situation. It is exceedingly important that any aid extended should be attended by scrutiny of the efficiency of operations.
Mr. Morrison, at page 600, in his summary puts it in this form:
A Canadian coal board should be established, to advise the government on assistance to the industry and protection of the public interest, and to administer such assistance as the government deems necessary.
There is this distinction. He thinks the government should determine the assistance necessary, and in my opinion perhaps the other two think it should be a function of the board. The second paragraph of the resolution reads as follows:
Provision is made further for the advisory functions of the board, for the employment of professional and technical advisers and assistants and their remuneration, and for all expenses of the act to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose.
I have now read it all. All I am urging now is that I am not in favour of this bill at this time, and I intend to explain why at this time I can see no necessity for it. If I had a much better idea than I now have or a much better idea than the minister has given me about it, I might then be in a position to support it. But what does it amount to? It is nothing more than a resolution saying that we should set up a new corporation to do what certain employees in the government, in the very language of the coal commission, have been doing satisfactorily over the years. At the moment I can see no reason whatever why these functions should not be performed by the men on the fuel board, one of whom I know very well and whom I regard as one of the greatest authorities on coal in the Dominion of Canada; he would certainly be better than any chairman the government can pick out of the air and put at the top of this board.
Dominion Coal Board

The point I am making ia that, at the moment and with the brief explanation we have had, I cannot see why we should go to the trouble or expense of creating a new corporation with all the attributes and functions- that is, aside from the civil service and so on-which attach to corporations of that kind.
I realize that what I am going to say will be quite unpopular with some people where I live, but I intend to say it anyway. What happens is this. We set up this commission, and I commend them for the immense amount of work they did. I also add that they could have found ninety-five per cent of this information in the files of the government right now. That could have been done, because I know it is there. All these vast summaries have been done again and again, as the minister pointed out, from the time we first started investigating this business many years ago. But that commission was appointed, and they are not blameworthy. They were appointed to find a national policy with respect to coal. I mean, in my own language that is the function for which they were set up. As is admitted by everybody, in discharging that function they have found no answer whatever. In this book there is no answer to the Canadian coal problem. It may be, as the minister said- and I think he is right because he has great knowledge of this business-that as far as central Canada is concerned, we must rely perhaps for a considerable time on imported coal. But he added that we got into an emergency a short time ago and had to switch railroad stock from other purposes in order to save this situation.
This whole thing comes down to a matter of dollars. The big problem is, is the coal problem in the Dominion of Canada a national problem, or is it not? I think we all admit that it is national. Then the only thing we have left to consider is whether it is worth while, I mean to provide the dollars necessary to give coverage to this country for our own coal. There is no doubt whatever that we have the coal. Unfortunately it lies largely on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, at least in that area right from the border away up through the coal branch to those mines in there. That difficulty may be insuperable. I must say I am discouraged; I have no ready cure to offer the minister at the moment. But it does seem strange that in a land like this, where we have the coal out there and the great need for it down here, we have developed no scheme by which those two elements may be brought together and thus create industry.

The minister covered our various fields, and I was very happy to hear him say what he did about Alberta. But in justice to those who operate fields in other parts of the country, let it not be forgotten that in Alberta they work under rather good conditions. You find seams anywhere up to sixteen feet in height. On the Highwood river, where I have been myself-I am not like the hon. member for Davenport; I have not travelled much, but that is only sixty-five miles from my home- I have seen seams of solid coal forty feet in thickness, and I may say that is quite a thick seam of coal. There you will find three and four seams underlying each other, perhaps three feet, six feet, eight feet and forty feet in thickness, all in the one formation. So that there is no problem there as to competition with any other place, one might say, with respect to price. Then on the coal branch, that is the branch running south, at Edson I believe they are stripping their coal, which, of course, means that the cost has been brought down to a very low figure. I understand that they operate both a deep mine and a strip mine at the same time. Then you come into Saskatchewan, about which the minister spoke; and if I am not mistaken the successful operation in that area is largely a stripping operation. Then he spoke of British Columbia. I am very far from being an expert in this business, and I am not referring to the district around Fernie, Shelley and so on, but is it not a fact that the Vancouver island field is practically worked out at the present time? I have not been there for several years, but at that time I was in very good company-[DOT]

I do not blame the minister for laughing. I was in the company of mining men; one of those places was available and we patronized it. The point I am trying to make is that at that time it seemed that those fields had practically reached exhaustion. Certainly it was a matter of not many years before they would reach the end of the blocked-out supplies.
Then the minister went to the maritimes. I am not going to say anything about that, save this. It seems to me that there of all places our national coal problem is simple. It is obvious that if things proceed as they have been proceeding in the last four or five years, as the minister says one can see the thing fading and disappearing as an industry at that place. As the minister stated, this coal commission has said that subsidies to the industry must cease, and I believe such steps have been taken. They do favour subven-

Dominion Coal Board
tions, by which they mean assistance with respect to freight rates in carrying the coal from one place to another. But I just wonder if at this time we can say that subsidies there should cease. As I said to the Minister of Labour in a previous debate in this house, and as the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply just repeated, down there the men blame management, the reason they give being inadequate machinery and inadequate power. On the other hand, management blames the men, saying they simply are not doing the work. The taxpayers have spent $20 million there by way of subsidies. As the minister has said, if we return to conditions as they were prior to the last war, then the industry can carry itself and pay a decent wage.
So, sir, with great respect I say I do not think we can ever thoroughly understand and, having done that, handle that problem unless we find out which of those statements is true. If it be that the ton and a half per man per shift, approximately, is the best that can be accomplished, then I think it is obvious that the worst fears of the minister will come true unless something more than subventions is done; and of course the only other thing is subsidies. But I do not see how this government or this parliament can say we should stop doing this or that until that specific and simple question is answered. And it can be answered; that can be done in a month by sending some experienced people down into those pits. The minister shakes his head. I do not often disagree with him; he is an authority on coal and many other matters, but perhaps I might get a little shot in somewhere edgeways. I say that can be solved by four men going under ground in those pits; I make that statement, and in it I have the support of a number of people engaged in the business with whom I have discussed it. Until we have that question answered, what are we doing? We are groping in the dark with respect to one of the greatest national problems facing us, and with respect to what may be one of our greatest assets if it can be properly and profitably handled.
Before we are through with this discussion I want the minister to tell me one thing. Having regard to the limitations on this board which I see in this resolution; having regard to the fact he has told us that the commission itself found that subventions had been satisfactorily handled in the past, what gain is there to anybody by transferring that function from officials of the department to a new and expensive corporation? That is a simple question which I think is worthy of an answer, and which I believe can be answered simply. I had something to do with
subventions in connection with the late Charles Stewart and the late Wesley Gordon. At different times I have come here with different sides of the coal industry trying to wangle subventions out of these people for certain areas, and I am very happy to say that at times I met with certain success. But I do not see how bringing a new face into the picture will make it any more efficient than it is at present, particularly when we have the finding in the report, as the minister said, that the subventions question has been well handled. The two commissioners have said that conditions change quickly; and at page 583 of the report they object to the statutory form. But let us remember that, as the minister has said, the money can be provided only by statute. If we should have a change in the business during the course of a year, when parliament is not sitting, I do not see why an official of the government, keeping in touch with and studying the matter, cannot make up his mind just as quickly as another official of the government who is called a corporation. I am utterly unable at the moment to see any necessity for setting up a board at this time.
I do not want any one to think I am speaking against the general recommendation that subventions to that industry be continued. I remember coming to Ottawa some years ago to appear before the railroad board. The results were bad, but now that we are to pay them better, perhaps my luck will change next time. I endeavoured to find out what it costs to haul a ton of coal from Drumheller, Lethbridge and the Crowsnest pass, first to North Bay and then to Toronto. The board made a finding and I admit that the figure was prohibitive. After that finding, the subvention situation was carried on.
May I say with respect that I do not think we yet know what the cost is. It is probably my fault that we do not. I was not good enough and I certainly did not have the same kind of help as the railroads had. I felt rather like a fool and I probably acted like one. I do not think anyone knows what it costs the railroads to haul a ton of coall from Cape Breton to Montreal or from Drumheller or the Crow to North Bay or Toronto. I believe there is an opening for our domestic coal in the area north of North Bay, but I cannot prove it. If we could really get down to it and find out what the cost of doing this thing was, then perhaps we might find a basis for a coal policy.
Coming back to where I started, I should like to have the minister explain, first, why the creation of a corporation and, second,

Dominion Coal Board
what more will this new group or body do or what more can they do than has been done already by some efficient people who at one time formed the dominion fuel board?

'Mr. Chairman, we have heard a lot about coal in this house during the past- years, and I think we agree with the minister's statement this afternoon that the coal industry in the maritime provinces is headed for disaster unless some satisfactory means can be found of putting it upon its feet. We all know what the situation has been during the last few months because of coal strikes and other things that have occurred. The hon. member for Calgary West has suggested that there are two alternatives; either the coal industry in the maritime provinces must be maintained, or it can be allowed to go down. He did not suggest that it be allowed to go down. We in the maritime provinces realize what a tragedy that would be. As the minister knows, there are about 100,000 of our people who are more or less dependent upon the coal industry in the maritime provinces and upon industries which, in turn, are dependent upon the coal industry.
As far as the setting up of this board is concerned, I am not familiar enough with the coal industry to say whether it should be set up. However I do know that as far as the dominion fuel board was concerned, there were certain parts of Canada, in my own province in particular, where it was felt that the board1 did not meet the situation. Whether the board proposed to be set up by the minister will meet the situation is something which I am not prepared to say. I know this action was recommended by the Carroll commission and I believe it has also been recommended by the operators and the workers in the coal industry.
There is no question that this industry has been kept alive by subventions and subsidies, but we in the maritime provinces feel that that is not any great favour. The minister mentioned that industry in the central provinces, apart from the coal industry, has been kept on its feet to a great extent and built up by the fiscal policies of this country and by our tariff. All industry has been helped greatly, and there is no reason in the world why the coal industry, which means so much to the eastern and western parts of this country, should not be assisted in the same way. The Carroll commission mentions that in its report
W het-her subventions and subsidies can best be handled by a board as suggested by the minister, or in some other way as suggested by the hon. member for Calgary West,

is something that I am not prepared to say. I understand that subventions were first given to the Nova Scotia Coal Company about 1930, in the depression years. Those subventions were given as a protection against United States coal. We must realize that Canada cannot produce, or at least she cannot deliver all the coal required in the country. At best we have never provided more than one-third, about 15,000,000 tons out of the 40,000,000 to 45,000,000 tons which are needed by industry and consumers. Therefore it is necessary to bring in coal from the United States. The subventions were given to assist in the movement of coal from Nova Scotia to Montreal and central Canada.
I should like to speak for a moment with reference to my own province. Subventions were given to the mines in Nova Scotia to assist in the introduction of coal into New Brunswick. The mines in New Brunswick depend entirely upon the local market. They sell their coal to the pulpwood industry, to the provincial hydro plants and to the railroads. Sufficient coal is mined in New Brunswick to provide a large portion of these needs. Because of the subventions paid to Nova Scotia mines to assist in the movement of coal into New Brunswick, the industry in New Brunswick has had a most difficult time. Coal from Nova Scotia, with the assistance of subventions, can be sold in New Brunswick more cheaply than New Brunswick coal. The subsidy paid on Nova Scotia coal to the Dominion Coal Company is about $1.67. There is a feeling among the smaller operators in the maritime provinces that the Dominion Coal Company, being a large and strong corporation, can get what they want while the smaller operators have always had a difficult time in getting anywhere near the same treatment as Dosco.
I wish to emphasize that I am not objecting in any way to the subsidies and subventions which have been paid in Nova Scotia, but in so far as the subventions apply to coal that is shipped to New Brunswick, we feel that they constitute an unfair discrimination. We submit that our people have not had the opportunities they should have had.
I should like to ask the minister whether it is the intention to appoint this board on a geographical basis, whether men appointed to the board will be men who understand the coal situation in western Canada, whether they will be men who understand the producers' and consumers' points of view. In New Brunswick the coal situation is entirely different from what it is in any other part of this dominion, and I should like to know whether New Brunswick will have a repre-

Dominion Coal Board
sentative on the board. How many members will constitute the board, and what technical advisers and assistants is it proposed to appoint?
We in the maritimes have been producing fifty-two per cent of the coal that is produced for sale in Canada, and in the sale of that coal the sellers have received about one-third of a cent per ton. But in western Canada, which produce forty-eight per cent of the total for the dominion, the sellers received 194 cents per ton. That just shows what a great difference there is between the different parts of this dominion. This board will have to be a very wise board indeed. It must understand the situation, in all parts of this country. I hope that something will be done to keep the coal industry on its feet and that every section of Canada which depends on the coal industry will receive consideration.

I have been in favour of protection, bonuses, subventions and subsidies for this great industry of coal ever since I entered this house, so that, we might develop in this country a national fuel policy and be dependent no longer on a United States supply, but on a supply of British coal, from Wales, from the maritime provinces in this country and from Alberta. At the time I was ridiculed and laughed at, but I had a powerful newspaper behind me, the Toronto Evening Telegram, which pioneered and was the author of this national fuel policy for Canada. In 1947, in some places we shall be using coal in Canada for ten months of the year on account of the unseasonable weather.
In 1915, when the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin was president of a great industry in Swansea, Wales, a ship came out and landed a cargo of Welsh coal in Ashbridge's bay, Toronto at the Baldwin granite plate plant. The Evening Telegram spent large sums of money in publicizing this importation of Welsh coal and generally an all-British fuel supply, and I introduced my resolution for a national fuel policy in the house in March, 1923. That same day Hon. Mr. Drury, then premier of Ontario, was in the building and denounced protection as an unmitigated evil that should be torn up by the roots. At that time we had very few supporters among hon. gentlemen opposite for a national fuel policy. I do not see any in the house who were here then. But Hance Logan and the present Mr. Justice Carroll of the coal commission, who was then a member of the house from Cape Breton, supported my resolution. It went to a committee of the House of Commons under the chairmanship of Mr. W. F. Carroll, M.P. That committee made a report, but the report was not adopted until five years later, after 83166-272
the election of 1926. About 1929, the government spent large sums of money by way of bonuses, subventions and subsidies for the coal industry. I give them credit for it, and we can see the results today.
I believe that the minister has done a great deal of good work. I am not one of those who think all the evils and all the good are confined to one party; far from it. I should like to see the functions of this board extended to cover wood peat and other forms of heating, because we shall have a difficult winter. People are going to freeze to death in Canada because of the scarcity of coal and wood. Passing on the train two or three weeks ago, I looked at the coal pile in Ashbridge's bay, Toronto harbour, in my constituency. Normally there will be 600,000 to 800,000 tons of coal piled up at the docks there, but there was very little coal there two or three weeks ago, on account of the strikes and the use of coal in June in some places. The coal situation the world over will be acute this winter. Many in Europe will freeze to death.
I have not the report of the coal commission before me, but I knew the chairman, Mr. Justice Carroll, when he was a member of this house and I had great confidence in him. I believe he has done great work as head of the coal commission, and its report contains a great deal of valuable information, and reveals a lot of labour spent on the problem. I just looked over it the other day; I hope to read it later.
Then think of the great riches of this country in water powers. We have a potential 47,000,000 horse-power in this country, of which only 7,000,000 horse-power has been developed and a portion of that 7,000,000 horse-power is used only seasonally, not for the whole twelve months of the year.
I support the principle of this bill and would like it to include a labour safety clause. I do not want any party to claim credit for it, but I like to pay credit where it is due, and protection was always Conservative doctrine, and in this form of it to pay bonuses, subventions and subsidies to be properly applied to the national development of the country and its resources. My hon. friends to my left were then, after the last election, about fifty-one in numbers in this house led by a very fine man, now a senator and a former cabinet minister, but I did not get very much support from his party at that time when their friends in Toronto, led by Mr. Drury, said that protection was an unmitigated evil.
Now let us get on with the business. In less than six months we shall be having the hardest winter we have ever had.

Dominion Goal Board

As I said, I hope the functions of this board will be extended to cover fuel, wood, peat, also cheap light and power. There is no reason why-only one-seventh of our potential horse-power
should be developed. There should be a national hydro policy for the whole dominion. A long time ago I was surprised to learn that they had no hydro electric policy in British Columbia, but they have established one recently. The province of Quebec is also starting on public ownership of hydro. I hope that in the years to come a national hydro electric policy will be developed for this whole dominion.
In the old days we used to have wood brought down by the old Nipissing railway from south of North Bay. This wood was used for fuel. A lot of it could be used now.
I hope that every effort will be made to see that this board which is to be appointed is the board which will expand itself as years go by and that we may get a national fuel policy which is needed for health purposes and to develop this country.

speechtext:
It is not my intention at this time to speak at any great length, but I should like to say that we must have a fuel policy before the difficulties of the country are solved. It was the hope of every hon. member, and certainly of those in the west who are particularly interested in coal production, that when the coal commission's report was brought down there would be some indication of a national fuel policy. I have gone carefully over the report and, so far as I can find out, there is nothing in it which would bring about a solution of that great problem. Whether the payment of subsidies will be the entire solution I am not sure. From my reading of the report I gather that the commissioners did not favour the idea of a production subsidy.
Like the hon. member for Calgary West, I am not in a position to say whether a production subsidy would be worth while. I do not think anybody is in a position to say that until he knows the actual facts. Certainly from my scrutiny of the report I did not think the commissioners were in a position to tell us, other than to say that conditions in the eastern part of Canada were not as good as they should be. I am not one of those, and never have been, who favour subsidizing inefficiency. It is poor business to start with, and it would be an exceedingly poor policy from the government's point of view.
The government has paid out large subsidies, particularly during the war, to get badly needed production. It subsidized production. During that time the government was spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in sub-

sidies; yet the report revealed that there was not the proper provision in the mines to warrant large payments in view of the fact that the companies themselves did not improve the working and safety conditions of the mines as they should have done. The result was that the miners who were compelled to work in these mines were working under a great handicap and in great danger. Whether the problem can be solved by the payment of subventions remains to be seen. I believe that by setting up this corporation the government would lead one to believe that subventions would be the solution. Whether that will prove to be true I am not certain, but I am certain of this, that whatever method the government intends to use to try to solve our coal problem it will have to see that steady employment is given in the mines. The solution will have to be one under which the miners themselves will be assured of steady employment the year around with sufficient income to keep them in a decent standard of living. That is fundamental. Whether it can be done by subsidy or by subventions I am not sure. It is a certainty that one of the great problems which we find in the west particularly is that of the long transportation haul.
If my memory serves me correctly-and I have hauled a great deal of coal-the mines in Alberta can produce coal at somewhere around $3 a ton. If you go out to the western part of the province in the foothills, I am told by good authority that coal can be put on the cars at around $1.50 a ton because, as the hon. member for Calgary West has indicated, of the great seams of coal in the banks. But whether it is $1.50, $2 or $3 a ton, the point I wish to make is that by the time the coal reaches Ontario there is a vast difference in the price. It jumps from the prices I have indicated to around $15, $16 and $17 a ton. I would assume that the difference is made up in transportation costs and so forth. Whether that can be overcome or not is a problem which remains for the government to solve.
As I have pointed out on many occasions, I think we missed one of the greatest opportunities this country ever had when during war time the government did not see fit to adopt the suggestion that some of us from the west made, namely, to create some industries out where this coal is to be found. If some of our larger industries were encouraged by the government to go out and establish themselves where the fuel is, it would be one of the things which would go a long way toward solving the problem which faces us. It is an easy matter to transport labour into the different parts of the country, much easier

Dominion Coal Board
than shipping coal these long distances. It seems a strange thing that a country so vast as Canada should have all its major industries centralized in a comparatively small area. In time of war particularly, that is a dangerous state of affairs. From the point of view of safety of the country, it would be a great advantage to have our larger industries scattered throughout the dominion. That is something which should be looked into by the government, and in way it might ease the subvention problem. I am certain of one thing, namely, that when the plan is made the government should pay particular attention to putting the mining industry on a solid and firm business foundation. We remember the days of the depression when the miners worked only 100 days a year. It is true that, while they were working, they received fairly good pay. I remember that when I was teaching in the mining district of Evansburg west of Edmonton-I spent quite a few years out there-the miners worked approximately 100 days a year. One would have to get exceptionally high wages, which they did not get, to carry him over a full year. That is one of the things that the miners fear today. They fear that the season will be extremely short for them, and they are looking ahead to the time when a depression will come upon them.
No matter what the government does, it must see to it that the operation of the mines will be such that the miners will earn enough to carry them over a full year. This will be a big job. I had hoped that when the commission brought down its report there would be something concrete in it for the government and for hon, members to go on in formulating a national fuel policy. I am extremely sorry to see that, in my view, the commission did not so report. The responsibility is on the government. I myself am not convinced that the shifting of the responsibility for this problem from the government to the corporation will be a solution. Something more concrete will have to be done. Nevertheless, when the bill comes down we shall see what is provided in that regard. Until the bill comes down I shall refrain from making any further remarks.

Like other speakers who have taken part in this debate, I was greatly disappointed to find that the report did not indicate any national fuel policy or even point out any avenues by which we might reach a satisfactory policy in that regard. I think we all agree that in this country we need a policy which, first, will keep the mines working the year around and, second, will make 8316G-2721
the country as self-sufficient as possible in coal. In this connection I have thought that we in Canada should do a great deal more in the matter of research to find means to reach these goals. I do not know just what amount of research is being carried on to discover new uses for coal. There is in Ottawa a small plant which carries on a certain amount of research, but I would suggest that plants should be established at the mines and that this is a matter which should receive a considerable amount of attention over and above what it has had so far.
Many people think the eventual solution of our fuel problem, in view of the fact that we have coal at the extremities of the country and none in the central parts where coal is most needed, will take the form of liquefication of fuel. I should like the minister to indicate what is being done in the matter of research into the possibilities along that line, how far they have been explored, and whether there is any idea of establishing pilot plants to devise new uses for coal at the mines on a sufficiently reasonable scale to ascertain whether such operations would be practicable and economic. The establishment of this coal board as called for by the resolution would seem to me to result in considerably increased expenditures without, so far as we have been, able to find out, any real improvement in the way in which things are carried on at present.
Before we get through with the bill, we should have some information from the minister as to what the increased expenditure will be as a result of the setting up of this board. I should think it would be considerable, and unless there are reasons which can be advanced to show that a great improvement in the whole coa.l picture can be brought about by the board, and savings effected by it, the increased expenditure is not warranted.

May I say a word on this? We, of course, are supporting this resolution that stands in the name of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, but I hope that the appointment of a board of this description will not be considered to have solved the problem. Dominion Coal Board,

This is, of course, a phase of economic planning. It frequently comes before the house in various forms, but it indicates over and over again that we must get down to a consideration of plans. speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary West asked a pertinent question. Freely translated, his question was, why is a dominion coal board any better than the dominion fuel board? The answer is that the coal board will have much wider terms of reference. The work of the board was wholly confined to carrying out the subvention policy which was formulated in 1922 and carried on with modifications until 1942.
It has been said that the subvention policy has been satisfactory, but that does not mean that it has been the cure-all for Canada's coal problem. It was a subvention policy which allowed coal to move from the mari-times into Quebec and sometimes into Ontario and, more recently, allowed a small tonnage of coal to move out of western Canada into northern Ontario. However, hon. members are aware that the subvention policy did not prevent the coal mines in the maritime provinces from being reduced to a working week of three days in certain years in the thirties. They know also that the subvention policy did not make for continuous employment in western Canada in certain periods. In other words, it was a good policy as far as it went, but it did not solve all the nation's coal problems.
