speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture, for the Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26S, to amend the criminal code.
He said: This is a bill which comes from the senate, where it has already been fully considered. It contains three amendments of importance, one on page 1, the second on page 2, and the third on page 3. The first has 'to do with an amendment we put through the session before last, I think it was, based upon actions taken during the war. Many years ago, I believe in 1912, a bill was brought in limiting horse racing, and allowing so many days each year on certain tracks. When that bill was brought in it was declared that all charters then in existence were continued in existence. During war time provision was made to transfer racing from tracks which were being used for other purposes for the time being to certain other tracks. Permission was granted for the transfer of perhaps seven days of racing from one track to another, and that was continued under legislation brought in two sessions ago.
In administering the act we discovered that some persons apparently found it was possible to make some profit by utilizing old charters, many of which had not operated since some time before 1912, and claiming the right to have seven or fourteen days of horse racing on the basis of those charters by transferring that racing from what had been an operating track at one time to some other track. When these requests were coming before me from time to time I finally concluded that I should not permit these old charters to be utilized for this purpose. So it was decided to bring the matter more up to date and to eliminate the possibility of using these old charters to transfer racing from one track to another, by stating that old charters not operative between January 1, 1938 and May 19, 1947 could not be used for the purpose of transferring racing from one track to another.
The second matter has to do with the holding of eight races daily under a charter. The old act provided that there could be eight races, one of which had to be a steeplechase. Very few horses in Canada are trained for steeplechasing, and the provision now is that of the eight races one may be a steeplechase, though not necessarily so.
The other provision makes it possible for trotting races to be held in the evening or under floodlights, as well as in the afternoon.
These are the three main provisions. The bill has been through the senate, where it was carefully considered, and I submit it for second reading.

My hon. friend shakes his head, but I have heard him use the argument time after time since he has been here in the house that price has something to do with this. Everyone admits that cheese is higher in price than butter at the present time, and much higher. If price is the only thing that counts, or the return that the farmer can get for it, then cheese production should certainly he higher. But everyone who knows anything about farming in Ontario knows the production season is at least a month late. The lateness of the season should have nothing to do with the freshening date of cows and that is what controls the production of cheese in Ontario. So that the lateness of the season has very little to do with the reduced production of cheese. The minister says that I shook my head last night. I am not going to speak at great length tonight, because I have spoken on this subject before, but this year will commemorate
Supply-Agriculture

a wonderful event. On July 24 next, in the city of Salt Lake, Utah, will be commemorated the hundredth anniversary of the inauguration of irrigation on the continent of North America. Two days before the 24 th of July, 1847, namely on July 22, the Mormon brigades were approaching the future site of that city. The leader of the Mormon brigade, Brigham Young, sent forward two or three men, led by Orson Pratt, and told them that when they arrived in the valley they were to dam a river flowing out of the mountains into that valley. The leader of the Mormon brigade himself and a major portion of the party arrived on the 24th, and this year that arrival will be celebrated by a great demonstration at a large monument which has been erected in Salt Lake City and which I hope myself to see late in October when I am on my way to the national reclamation association's meeting at Phoenix, Arizona.
That event inaugurated irrigation on the continent of America, and within two or three days after July 24, 1847, five acres had been reclaimed and put under irrigation. With them it was an absolute necessity. The season was late, but of course the climate was favourable. The soil was exactly the same as we have in Alberta and Saskatchewan, wonderful soil that will grow anything, but it was without water. They began at once to work; they worked very hard, and in the ensuing eighteen years, that is to say up to 1865, they had constructed over 1,000 miles of irrigation canals and had reclaimed roughly 150,000 acres of land.
The results have been phenomenal. Anyone who knows Utah knows it is largely a mountainous state, with tremendous mountains and a few valleys, one of which is the great Salt Lake valley; yet, although it has only an area of 84,000 square miles-that is not a large area-the population today is about 550,000. That is a remarkable demonstration of what can result from an irrigation programme, and I am convinced that the same results would accrue in both Alberta and Saskatchewan if this house would support the minister-I believe it would-in an endeavour to inaugurate a programme comparable with what has been accomplished over there.
Last fall I had the high honour-it was a high honour to me, a very humble person- to be invited by the national reclamation bureau of the department at Washington to attend a function at Omaha, at which I learned a great deal about the tremendous results, beneficial results they have been too, that have accrued throughout the seventeen dry western states by water conservation and irrigation. There are seventeen states that are afflicted with low moisture, like our own

western provinces. When the function was over I was invited to go with a body of engineers and statisticians, which I was glad to do, to survey the great improvements in the valley of the Platte river. The Platte river is very much like the Saskatchewan river. It has two great branches, the North Platte and the South Platte. They both rise in the mountains and join away down in Nebraska, flowing into the Missouri river, much like the Saskatchewan. We have two great branches rising in our own Rocky mountains and flowing down, joining in the province of Saskatchewan and on into Lake Winnipeg.
I am in deadly earnest in my desire to do anything I can, as long as I am in public life, to assist in the reclamation of the western provinces and to further the whole economy of those provinces. And it can be done through irrigation. On that journey up and down the Platte river valley we ascended right up into the mountains. There were reservoirs 10,000 or more feet high up in the mountains on the North Platte particularly, and on the South Platte about 12,000 feet high in the mountains, to the everlasting springs from which the water rises and flows on down across the prairies. Many gigantic dams and reservoirs have been constructed there. I am not going to describe them as I should like to do, because I do not want to hold up the minister's estimates. On the North Platte, in the mountains, there are four gigantic dams. Up in the mountains themselves there are three gigantic dams, and there is one down in the foothills, namely, the Seminoe, the Pathfinder, the Alcova, the Kingsley and the Guernsey. The first three reservoirs conserve about
2,500,000	acre feet of water which is being used down on the dried-out prairies; the fourth, the Kingsley, contains over 2,000,000 acre feet of water; the next one, the Guernsey, contains about 50.000 acre feet. I am sure that altogether on the North Platte over 5,000,000 acre feet of water are contained in the reservoirs for irrigation purposes. On the South Platte something marvellous has been done.
I must confess that I am not in favour of diverting water from one watershed into another, but what is done in the United States is not for me to criticize. However, a branch of the Colorado river was diverted and the water taken through the high mountains, through a thirteen-mile tunnel. The amount of water taken through there is 550 cubic feet per second. It is pumped up to the level of the tunnel. Once through the mountains, it goes down 2.900 feet, passing through five power-houses on the way. In the course of its descent it produces 250,000 horse-power,

Supply-Agriculture
part of which, namely, that from the first power-house in the foothills, goes back over the mountains to supply the power that pumps the water up. It is the only place I know of where perpetual motion is achieved as a result of electricity.
East of the mountains themselves there are three large reservoirs, the Horsetooth, Carter lake and Flatiron. These three together conserve water which comes through the mountains to the extent of 350,000 acre feet. From them the water flows out through the irrigation canals. The transformation there has been stupendous. I should like it if this whole house could be taken to the Platte basin so that * they could see with their own eyes the marvellous transformation which has been made in those three states of Colorado, Nebraska and Wyoming; they are states which are just as dry as the driest part of southern Alberta or the driest part of Saskatchewan. In many cases the water must be pumped up. It can be done in Saskatchewan. When I was making a survey between Elbow on the Saskatchewan and Moose Jaw and Regina, someone asked me if the water could be pumped up to irrigate the higher areas. It could be. It has been done over there in the United States, and the results have been stupendous.
In a word, what are the results? If one travels west across our own prairies, after leaving Winnipeg the next place of any consequence is Portage la Prairie, and then Brandon. Then you go a long distance until you come to Regina. From Regina the next place is Moose Jaw. Then you go another long distance to Swift Current. Then from Swift Current you go to Medicine Hat where you enter a really dried-out area. It is pitiable to see the territory around Medicine Hat,; it is magnificent land but without water. Then, after another long distance, you come to Lethbridge. That, I believe, is somewhere near 800 miles, using an arbitrary number, in which we have those few cities, every one of them struggling for life, except Lethbridge, [DOT]because the country roundabout, although it is productive, lacks water. It may have a good deal this year, but we cannot count on years like this. We have too much water in. Ontario this year, but we do not want to count on this very often.
In the same distance, Mr. Chairman, in the Platte basin there are forty fine towns and cities. All of them are rich; all of them are growing and all of them are extremely prosperous. All roundabout is an agricultural area the like of which I never saw before. If one drives into any of these cities in the Platte basin, what does one find? Take, for instance,
Scottsbluff. I suppose very few hon. members have ever heard of Scottsbluff, but I drove into it at night time from another city on the prairies called Alliance, and I thought I was going into New York city, for ten miles out of Scottsbluff every farmhouse, barn and farmer's yard were lit up. I asked the chauffeur, on one occasion when we were about eight miles out of Scottsbluff if we were in the city. "Oh, no," he said, "we have eight miles yet to go." That power is produced as the water tumbles down from one level to a lower, so that not only do they have irrigation which produces tremendous crops and provides ample fodder- for all their large herds-and their herds are extremely large- but it produces electric power. We can do the same thing in the west.
If one wants to see a demonstration of what is being done in the west in the way of power production, he just needs to start at Banff and go as far as the city of Calgary. I believe the company is called the Calgary Power Company. The water coming down the Bow basin passes through three, if not four, powerhouses and produces a great deal of electricity. That can continue on down the river. Much of these prairies can not only be irrigated and at least three to five million acres reclaimed but can be lit up. I know of no other way in which we can save these prairies. It is the most heart-breaking thing to read that in the last five years, in the three prairie provinces in Canada-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-the population has decreased by
104.000	souls. This means that our three prairie provinces, which have a combined area of 705,000 square miles, have gone down to approximately 2.350,000 persons.
What has happened in the Platte basin? I believe that Colorado, Nebraska and Wyoming have a combined area of about 278,000 square miles or thereabouts. But those three states have a population of 2,700,000 as compared with the population in our three provinces in the west. If our three western provinces are to be reclaimed there must be a similar programme undertaken there. I am convinced of this, and I would give my strongest support to any such programme. I do not care what government it is that does it; any government that will bring in a programme to reclaim these prairie provinces I will support to the limit. What has been the result in the United States? Just as I have said. On those 278,000 square miles there are more than 300,000 more people living on those bald-headed United States prairies, and part of them covered with mountains, than on our
705.000	square miles in our own three western provinces.

If the same ratio of population were distributed over Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta as now live in Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming, our three prairie provinces would have a population of 7,000,000. They should have that population, and will have it if they get fair play. What does that mean? It means another forty towns and cities as firm buyers of products made in the east. I like to couple up both east and west, because the more the prairies grow, the more their cities and towns boom and prosper, the better it is for us here. In many addresses I have delivered during the last year both in the east and in the west in the advocacy of programmes such as this, I have found everyone unanimously in favour of reclamation both in the maritime provinces and in the west.
The minister of course knows how far he can go, but I am sure he, as a westerner would have far more influence in the cabinet than anyone else-and so he should have-as far as the western reclamation programme goes. I wish this whole reclamation programme were under his department. It is now divided between the reconstruction department and agriculture; but the problems, the needs and the requirements of the prairies are matters in which his voice should be paramount in the cabinet. To me it is a terrible tragedy, as I said a moment ago, to see the population go down and down because, Mr. Chairman, that means fewer buyers for the threshing machines and agricultural equipment made in your own fine little towns of Seaforth, Clinton, Goderich, and other eastern centres. But if the population went up instead of down it would mean more buyers and more jobs down here. We in Ontario and Quebec go forward as these outlying parts of the country go forward. The man who cannot see that we all expand together cannot see very much.
The matter of water conservation and irrigation is not a matter of cost, it is an extremely sound investment, as I proved a moment ago by pointing out the increase in population in those three dried-out western states of the United States. Over there they are so thrilled with their towns and villages in the dried-out areas, always growing and expanding; towns and cities like Scottsbluff-Greeley, Alliance, and I could name a dozen or two more, each with many secondary industries. We should have exactly the same thing m our own west. Every town and city in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba should have several times the secondary industries they have today; and they would have those industries if they could get water for the prairies. And they can get it; the Saskatchewan river can supply it.

So I support this vote, as I will support the other vote under the reconstruction department when it is brought in. I hope the minister will press hard not only for the completion of the dam on the St. Mary river, as he will be doing in a moment or two, but for the construction of other dams. Why allow all that God-given water, that rich resource of water, to flow down to the sea and do no good as it moves across the prairies? So it is a delight on my part, knowing, as I believe I do, what can be achieved out there, to support this and any other vote that will mean reclamation and conservation of our own western prairies.
I expect that when I come back from Phoenix next fall I shall have a more extended story to tell, because when I am down there I shall thoroughly survey the marvellous transformation that has taken place in Arizona, Nevada and southern California, where today they are spending or rather investing millions of dollars. One has only to look at the gigantic works they are completing to increase the productivity of their soil to realize the benefits that will accrue from the programmes they are carrying on right now. I believe they are so satisfied with the tremendous achievements that have so far been completed that they are now initiating another great programme, on which they have many engineers working, for the reclamation of the whole Missouri valley. That is expected to cost about $2 billion, and they expect to increase the population of that valley by several millions. From the many miles I have travelled on the lower Missouri river, it seems to flow very largely through a flat country, where there would not seem to be many opportunities for the development of power; but their programme calls for the development of over 2,000,000 horse-power of electrical energy on the Missouri river and the reclamation of an additional 5,000,000 acres of land. Just think what that will mean, taking 100 acres per farm. That will mean 50,000 farms, which, at the Colorado average of nearly twenty people to each 100 including those in towns and cities, would mean a tremendous increase in population. The average here in Canada is from five to ten; so just look at what it would mean if we should ever reach the Colorado average of twenty per 100 acres. So I say this is not a cost but an investment. If I were sitting in the minister's place-as I never could, knowing nothing whatever about agriculture and being unable even to attempt to answer the questions he is asked, although I can answer a great many questions concerning matters I know something about-I would come in here with a gigantic programme of

I should like to make one or two remarks with regard to the recital which has just been made to the committee. When I was a boy I had the privilege of living in the area of which the hon. member has been speaking. We lived for five years in the valley of the Platte, close to where it joins the Missouri, but we were starved out and came back to Ontario. The conditions which existed there in the early part of the nineties were almost identical with the conditions that existed in Saskatchewan and Alberta in the early part of the thirties. The same conditions prevailed in Nebraska and Kansas in the thirties of this century as prevailed there in the nineties of the last century. There has been no difference in the weather conditions. We had exactly the same conditions in western Canada in the nineties as they had in Nebraska, and as we had in Saskatchewan during the thirties. There is nothing new

about it. Those conditions have prevailed on a number of occasions and they will come back again. Some provision must be made for the better distribution of the water that is in that country if people are going to live there.
I have driven the whole length of the Platte in recent years since these dams were built. I may say that some of the cities spoken of were there before irrigation wa3 put in, but they were in much the same position at that time as some of our cities in western Canada; they were going down in population rather than up, but now it is a different story with irrigation. In driving from one end of the Platte river to the other one can discover many of the things we should do and also some of the things that perhaps we should be careful not to do. I do not know whether the hon. member visited the higher lands where you can see the foundations of houses that were put up when the irrigation scheme was first put through.

That did not occur
around Alliance, which is a city of from 15,000 to 18,000 people. They pump the water up, but the land is thoroughly irrigated and they have marvellous crops.

One can see the foundations of houses that were built and the remains of old cars beside those basements. I made a point of going to see that, because there are some things they have done in the United States that we should avoid. The story they tell there is that the contractors were obliged to make a declaration that water had passed through the ditch before they could get paid and they say that some water was taken through in bottles behind horses. Of course that was in the earlier days of the undertaking. I think that story is an exaggeration of what actually happened, but the ditches are there and there is no water in them; the foundations are there, but there are no buildings on them; the old cars are there that were worn out in the district and no one is using them. This is all up in the higher lands which are much higher than Nebraska or the eastern part of Montana. As I say, that area is the exception.
One can learn from that there are acres and acres of land, hundreds of square miles or even thousands of square miles of land in western Canada as well as in the western states on which you cannot put water, or if you do you waste it. The sub-soil of the area of which I was speaking is gravel and it is very high. One dropping there from an areo-plane and not knowing anything about the altitude would think he was on the prairies
[Mr. Gardiner.[
up north of the boundary, but he would find that he was probably up three or four times as high as the prairies. That also has some bearing on the question of what one can do.

I wish to bring to the minister's attention a much more modest request under this item. For some years I have brought to his attention the desire of the people of the Peace River block to have P.F.R.A. applied to that section of the community. I have asked for this several times, last year on several occasions, and if I recall the minister's answer aright it was to the effect that he had intended extending the application of P.F.R.A. to practically all western Canada and practically all Canada, but that he had been prevented from going ahead because of the unsettled state of dominion-provincial matters. But in view of the fact that British Columbia and Alberta have come to satisfactory tax arrangements with the federal government, we feel that we should not be punished because some other provinces have not done that.
The minister is, I am sure, well aware that the farmers in the area to which I have referred have petitioned his department and passed resolutions time and time again, year after year, asking for the application of P.F.R.A. to their area. I have explained to the minister-I do not think it is necessary because he knows it just as well as I do- that there are peculiar conditions in that area. There are very few wells to be had either for watering stock or for water for the homes. People have to melt ice in the winter for water and often have to haul their water for miles from the river to do their washing and water their cattle. In the summer, the area is fairly
well supplied with rain, which helps to grow crops, but they have not water for their stock, and they want to use the privileges which P.F.R.A. makes available in the west where it now applies.
Is it the intention to extend the application of P.F.R.A. to the Peace River block under the present vote, and, if not, can the minister say when it will be possible to extend it to the Peace River block? I can assure him that there are thousands of farmers who will be anxiously waiting to hear his answer to that question. I do not want to hold up the estimates by making any emotional pleas, but I hope that the minister will give this matter his serious consideration.

In reply to the question that has just been asked, all I can say is what I did say in making the announcement a short time ago, namely, that P.F.R.A. would not be extended this year and that the government intended to undertake expenditures under votes which would be in the supplementary estimates. Those expenditures are to be made in the maritime provinces on the marsh lands that are dyked and on some special projects in British Columbia, one of which is under way and by the way is in the constituency of my hon. friend. The other amount is to be utilized in the areas of the western provinces which are not under P.F.R.A., which includes the Peace River district of British Columbia, and also in the eastern provinces. That expenditure is not intended to be on the same type of work that we are doing under P.F.R.A., the reason being that the responsibility for that type of work has always been with the provinces. As members from the western provinces and also from the eastern provinces know, works of that kind, such as finding water for household use, have been carried on provincially or municipally. In Saskatchewan, for example, which I know best, the provincial government through the department of public works or the highways department provided nearly all the dug-outs and dams that were built there prior to P.F.R.A. That is, they assisted in the building of them, or the farmers put them in themselves individually. In some places municipalities had equipment to assist the farmers in doing the work. So far as wells are concerned, the territorial government, before even the provinces were formed, dug wells, and they can be seen in-the older settled areas of western Canada today, most of them being on the road allowances. If one starts digging wells for people and you do not dig the well as close to one house as you do to another there is trouble. Sometimes the water is not located as close
Supply-Agriculture

to one house as it is to another, and so it was thought good politics, if not good business, to dig the wells on the road allowance and let everybody go to it for their water.
These practices were carried on under local organizations, not from Ottawa. Any activities that have been in eastern provinces or in western provinces, outside the P.F.R.A., have been carried on under provincial governments, or provincial governments working in cooperation with municipalities or counties. We said last year and again this year that until there is some further agreement than we have up to the moment with regard to responsibilities of that kind, the dividing of responsibilities, and the dividing of responsibility for collecting taxes, probably we should not take on any long-term policy in connection with this particular matter. Therefore we have undertaken to carry on P.F.R.A. where it is now being carried on in the Palliser triangle, and decided to bring these other water expenditures to bear upon the problems that exist there in so far as we think we ought to enter into agreements with the provinces to carry them on. I am not in a position to say the amounts that will be in the supplementary estimates which will be brought down in a few days. I know how much we have submitted to the treasury board. In a few days these estimates will be brought down and we shall know how much the amount is.

I do not wish to make a long speech on this matter, since I made reference to it on March 6 during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, but I wish to refer to the fact that up until May 22 we had hoped-I am speaking for the members from British Columbia-that the same principle as exists under the P.F.R.A. should be extended to our province. The reason I want to go back to that point again is that in his statement-to which the minister has just referred-which he made on May 22 and which he has elaborated tonight to some extent, he seemed to imply that it is not contemplated in any way to extend to British Columbia a thorough-going scheme of land reclamation and irrigation, but rather that it would be small local projects such as might be brought forward from time to time by the provincial government. I suggest to the minister-he no doubt has the advice of experts, and I am not going to put myself up against them-that the type of country which we have, particularly in the interior of British Columbia, does not lend itself to these small, local schemes. Speaking on the 6th of March, I said, and I am still of the opinion, and am [iMr. Gardiner.]
supported by all the briefs and expert opinions which I have been able to read, that what is needed is something in the nature of what they call in the United States an integrated project for the development of water power and irrigation as well as land reclamation. In the dry belt areas of the interior of British Columbia where you cannot divert a stream to irrigate large tracts of flat land but require to pump water probably 100 feet up to the bench above the river, you need water power for these projects. That is why it is so disappointing to us to read the statement which the minister made on May 22 and to find that he said, as reported at page 3318 of Hansard:
The dominion government would be prepared to discuss with the provinces concerned plans under which development could proceed over a period to be agreed upon, sufficiently long to bring about the desired results, but not to exceed five years.
That seems to me to indicate a very short-range and local project which will not fill our needs.
I wish to bring to the minister's attention one particular brief which has been submitted, and of which I know he has received a copy. It was submitted by the association of British Columbia irrigation districts. After going into the principles which they felt should apply in this' type of work, they set forth a summary of the acreage available for irrigation under some such thorough-going scheme. They show that there is a total of 97,155 acres available throughout the dry-belt portion of the interior of British Columbia. In my opinion that does not include actually all the land which is available, because no mention is made of the land between Kamloops and Ashcroft on the Thompson river. There was, for instance, once a project at a place called Walhachin, where their objective was a million boxes of fruit a year. They developed an irrigation scheme, but it was all by bringing water down in ditches some twelve or fifteen miles from lakes back in the hills. Then one year the ditches washed out; there was found to be no more money available from the private interests who were behind the scheme, and the thing folded up. You can drive through a tremendous area of derelict fruit trees where they were within a hair breadth of realizing their objective of a million boxes of fruit a year, when this happened, and today there is hardly a soul about. Nothing has since been done. It proves conclusively that you cannot put in an irrigation scheme if you expect the land which is brought under irrigation to bear all the costs without some government assistance. That is why the thing folded up. They did not

Supply-Agriculture
have enough money left in the treasury; they had not enough back from the sale of the land when the ditches washed out. There is all this tremendous acreage available down our river valleys and lying back from the rivers, but they require pumping from the land itself up to the bench lands before it can be got under way.
I have had a lot of correspondence with the minister and with other departments. I wish to refer to it and to ask the minister some questions in elaboration of has statement. The correspondence which I have had was with the Department of Public Works, the Department of Agriculture and, to a lesser extent, with the Department of Fisheries trying to get all the departments concerned with the rivers in British Columbia to work in with the British Columbia government with this idea of an integrated project. In one of his replies the minister indicated that he did not feel his department had any interest in that particular matter. I have, however, a letter from the Minister of Public Works on this subject in which he says his department is going ahead to appoint a commission in consultation with the provincial government to investigate conditions on the Fraser and Thompson rivers. He says:
A decision has already been reached to proceed in this matter and the provincial government and interested departments of the federal government are being approached in connection with the personnel of the proposed board or commission.
It does seem to me that if that is being done, here is a favourable opportunity for the two departments concerned, in conjunction with the provincial government, to work out some such scheme. All that we ask at the moment is that a survey be made. Look at the land available and decide how best we can bring it under irrigation and build up the water power necessary to pump the water and provide electric light, power and so on. I know there are engineers of the department of the P.F.R.A. out there now working with the Department of Veterans Affairs. That is another reason why I think the Department of Agriculture and the P.F.R.A. should be interested, because in that area the Department of Veterans Affairs is settling a number of veterans on the land. That is a dominion responsibility, not solely a provincial responsibility. The potentialities of that area are so tremendous that once we get the water on the land, although it might cost a lot of money-I know I have advocated economy-it would more than repay the cost over the years. The proceeds from the development of the land and the bringing in of secondary industries would more than
repay any initial capital expenditures. If it were regarded as a continuing project, a long-range project, we would find that we would recoup more than any outlay which was made in the first place. I hope that the minister will reconsider the statement which he made on May 22 and take under consideration again the institution of a full-scale integrated project in conjunction with the Department of Public Works and the provincial government.
In his statement the minister referred to certain projects related to farm lands in British Columbia, and I should like to know whether that is the Pemberton Meadows project, to which he referred a moment ago, in what is now the Cariboo constituency.
That is one of them.

I believe the engineers
of the P.F.R.A. are doing service in the Thompson valley around Chase and Pritchard for the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Yes.
Have they any other work going on there at the present time?

There are about six
projects in British Columbia which are being investigated for soldier settlement.

Has the provincial government brought forward yet any projects following the statement the minister made on May 22 when he indicated that the dominion government would be prepared to discuss with the provinces any project which they might advance?

The government of

A final question. Are the
P.F.R.A. officials doing anything directly in conjunction with the Department of Public Works along the lines of the letter I read from the Minister of Public Works with regard to a commission to inquire into flood control and other conditions on the Fraser river and the Thompson river watershed?
There has been correspondence back and forth between the minister and myself iSith regard to the possibilities, not only in British Columbia, but in some of the other provinces as well.

I should like to get certain information from the minster for purposes of clarification, because I am not as optimistic in this matter as the Prime Minister seemed to be about getting out on the 8th of July, if one may judge from some of

the speeches tonight. It is not clear to me what the minister intends to do in British Columbia under this act. This is a serious matter in the Fraser valley and I submit that this act should be extended to cover it. I am disappointed in any statement the minister has made so far. Probably what the minister had in mind in that regard was that some organization would be set up to survey the whole field and determine where the responsibility lies in connection with many of these works. There is a division of authority and responsibility as between the province and the dominion with regard to these matters, which makes it impossible for anyone to make any general 
statement about what this government will do, or what the provincial government will do; and until someone has determined that, it will be impossible for me to say what projects we shall work on, or how many. I only know that we shall work on as many as we have money to cover, and that will be determined in the usual way. Votes will be brought before the house and submitted for discussion, and then that money will be spent on whatever it is provided for.
Has the minister in mind any general principles governing the sort of project he would be prepared to work on with the provincial government?

We have one which we have already done, or it is almost done, and that is the Pemberton Meadows lands. That one is now practically finished. The expenditure there was all made by the federal government. No assistance was given by the province at all in that. There may be special reasons why that was done by the federal government. Those reasons may not exist elsewhere. Each project would have to be considered on its merits and dealt with accordingly, but it is that type of thing. The work being done there is the work of keeping water off the land instead of putting it on, as was stated by the hon. member for Fraser Valley.

How do you
approach the government to get a grant similar to that in connection with Pemberton Meadows? Is it through this department? The minister says there is to be some money available for this, and I believe he spoke of six projects. Who will settle what these projects are, the federal government or the provincial government?

These projects that have .been spoken of are not under our department at all but under veterans affairs, and we have been giving services of that kind, not only to other departments of this government, but to provincial governments and municipalities, in connection with water matters, by utilizing the engineering staff we have under P.F.R.A. When we do provide that engineering staff to investigate, it does not necessarily follow that we shall spend money on it. The Pemberton Meadows investigation started three or four years ago. We had a vote of S10.000 to provide for covering the expenses of sending engineers there. They went and investigated, and we finally undertook that work on our own, largely because it was almost altogether soldier settlement put 1here by the federal government following the first war. We under-

took to control the water on the lands, because it was running over the lands that these men had. This was a special condition that existed, which we undertook to deal with. Each one of these projects, or any projects that we undertake there, will have to be dealt with on their merits. In his statement the minister said it was considered that there were certain works outside the drought area which, if undertaken, would be of assistance to all Canada through making possible increased developments of farm lands which, if left to provincial or municipal responsibility, might greatly retard Canada's development. Can the minister amplify that statement? Are there any characteristics or particulars which the department has in mind and which such lands must fulfil before anything can be done?
. Mr. GARDINER: I had in mind, when making the suggestion to the government, which was accepted, that this expenditure would relate largely to the opening up of new lands for settlement purposes. That settlement may be a movement of people out of Montreal into northern Quebec; it may be moving people from one part of the province to another or from one province into another; or it may be bringing in new settlers altogether. They are projects of a type which may make for further development of the country.

I have been following the minister's estimates through from the beginning and I think they are all justified. Particularly do I approve the estimates for the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. If I were to offer any comments on those expenditures I would suggest that they be increased rather than reduced. For some years I have been advocating the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act so that its provisions would render some assistance in solving the problems which the eastern farmers are trying to deal with. I refer particularly to the flooding of the dyke lands and to the damage and destruction wrought on our meadows and intervale lands along our rivers and streams.
I notice that the hon. member for Fraser Valley referred to a specific case, and I imagine I may be pardoned if I do likewise and refer to one which has been brought to my attention for several years. It is the damage and destruction that is done to our meadow lands along the Margaree river. Every year acres of that most fertile land in
the maritime provinces have been rendered unproductive and acres of it have been washed away by flood waters, by ice floes and by uncontrolled waters which the farmers have been trying to control. They have now reached their limit. Knowing the situation as I do,
I will say for these farmers that they have done their very best to deal with the ravages of these destructive agencies, but a point has now been reached where this damage and destruction cannot be controlled by individual efforts. I do not know through what means or through what department some assistance can be rendered, but I honestly believe that, unless some government assistance is given, the most fertile lands of the Margaree valley will be washed out into the Atlantic ocean.
I believe that the assistance which could be rendered to combat those agencies would not mean a great contribution from the government. If the government were to assist the farmers, those who have vested holdings there, to build at strategic points breakwaters, small protecting walls, sheer dams and to do a little bit of dredging in order to keep the river in its natural channel, I believe that a great deal of the damage could be prevented. I honestly believe that if some such assistance is not rendered to our farmers in that particular section of the country, that fertile land in the Margaree valley, which is one of the most productive in the whole of the maritime provinces, will be washed away into the Atlantic ocean.
I would urge upon the Minister of Agriculture, although possibly this remedial measure does not come under the authority of his department, to collaborate with some other department of the government and point out to them the emergent need of conserving this fertile land. It is all right to be undertaking to rehabilitate lands which are today unproductive. But when we have productive land which has been destroyed by these damaging agencies, it is just as important to preserve land that is in productivity now a3 it is to spend money to rehabilitate land that is out of production. I would urge the minister to collaborate with the department which has to do with this matter, to impress upon them its emergency nature, and the necessity of something being done to assist our honest farmers who are trying their best and have exceeded their means in endeavouring to preserve these holdings.

The matter which has just been referred to has been brought to our attention and has been under consideration by the different departments. Might I suggest that we could discuss these projects we are now discussing to much better advantage ' when the supplementaries come down, which
Supply-Agriculture

will be very shortly, when we shall know just what amounts of money are being voted. We can then discuss the expenditures of these moneys. If the committee would agree, now that we have had a sort of general discussion on the question, I think we could then enter much more intelligently into a discussion of these projects when the amounts voted for them are before us.

Originally I had
intended to speak at some length on this item, but I think I shall spare hon. members inasmuch as they are trying to get along in a hurry. However I think this parliament should realize that in western Canada there are still large semi-desert areas. Unless we do something to reclaim those areas in the very near future, our national economy may be in danger. From history we know that these droughts come along, roughly, every seven or ten years. We realize, therefore, that we are probably due for another one of these droughts fairly soon. Since coming to parliament, I have found it difficult to understand why, every year, we talk about irrigation, but do very little about it. Canada's behaviour in this regard compares unfavourably with that of the United States. Back in 1935, drought conditions in the United States were even worse than they were in western Canada. Whole areas had turned into dust bowls. People were moving out and going on relief. But since 1935, the United States have irrigated about 5,000,000 acres and have begun plans or actually started construction for the irrigation of about 10,000,000 other acres. Yet we in Canada have irrigated only about 155,000 acres. I certainly do not think this compares favourably with what has been done in the United States. As far as I can see from what the minister has said tonight, I do not think the reasons or the excuses he has given for not proceeding are sufficient. I suppose lack of funds is the main reason. I think the S3,000.000 we are bringing down in the estimates tonight is disgraceful, to say the least, for meeting this western problem.
This S3.000.000 has nothing to do with the projects my hon. friend is discussing.
I realize that.
Unless it may be a small part for engineering.
I realize that; but that is the amount we are giving for irrigation.
No, that is not irrigation.

There may be a few Trillions more; I do not know. I will not argue with the minister about that tonight. But last year, two years ago, I saw this parliament vote in gifts and loans almost $2 billion for the reclamation of other countries, and probably most of those amounts were justified. If we could give so much to these other countries I do not see why we cannot find a few million dollars for a project so badly needed here at home, and one which would be self-liquidating. In the war years we spent SI 10 million, which I think was the amount mentioned by the minister as the total sum required for western irrigation, in a few weeks; yet here we cannot find that much money for this work today. Recently President Truman said that probably there would soon be great benefits from the St. Lawrence river project. I think that is so, and I believe many Canadians would support it; but many westerners would find it difficult to vote for that project before getting the irrigation they need. I think easterners are . going to need that project just as much as westerners, because, as the hon. member for Davenport has said, they will soon need markets. During the war years our factories increased their capacity by about forty per cent, and we know that when the Canadian loans are gone some of these foreign countries will not be able to continue to buy from Canada. Where are the eastern manufacturers to sell their products when that time comes. I suggest to hon. members from the east that perhaps then they will be glad to have people living in these irrigated areas on the prairies, who will be able to use some of their manufactured products.
I have several questions I should like to ask the minister in this connection. In my constituency we have been waiting years for something to be done in connection with, irrigation.

May I suggest that those matters come under the next item. Could we pass the rehabilitation item and go on to irrigation, what comes next? The St. Mary river dam is the first of the big projects, and it is the next item. If the question my hon. friend has in mind has to do with the Saskatchewan river project, and other similar projects, they are not provided for in this item.

All right; I will leave those questions until then. But I want to-ask the minister one question which I am quite sure applies to this item. A few months ago I had the privilege of hearing the min-

ister speak about irrigation. A few nights before that, he had spoken in Lethbridge, and the Financial Post reported him in this way:

Will the minister tell us if that is to be over a long period of years, with just a little coming through each year, or if we are to get that $100 million some time soon. Will he tell us, furthermore, whether the government is waiting to use this irrigation programme as a post-war project?

In view of the minister's statement that the reclamation work in the maritimes would be better discussed on the items in the supplementary estimates, I shall reserve what I have to say until that time; but I would point out that, as far as the repairing of dykes in the maritime provinces is concerned, it is a matter of urgent necessity. Time is really of the essence in connection with the work there, because these dykes are disintegrating, not only every year, but every month. When the supplementary estimates are brought down this year I hope they will not be simply for investigation, but that there will be something for the reconstruction of the dykes in the maritimes.

The provincial ministers have already been here. Mr. Taylor, minister of agriculture of New Brunswick, was here. Mr. McKenzie was not able to come, but his deputy was here, and we have discussed the possibilities in connection with expenditures for this year. An amount is being placed in the supplementary estimates. I am not at liberty tonight to say what that amount is, but I can discuss it freely at that time.

The members of this group have a very high appreciation of the work done under P.F.R.A. in the past and at the present time, but we feel that the time has come for the government to launch larger scale projects than have been undertaken in the past. We particularly feel that the conservation of the waters of the Rocky mountain watershed is of paramount importance, not merely to western Canada, but to the whole of Canada. While it was not possible to do anything along that line during the war, we believe that the time has now come when the government should undertake that
work. We consider it important that irrigation projects should not be looked upon as a form of relief works for the purpose of providing employment. I believe the minister will agree with that statement, but I am not so sure the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will agree with it, because I understand his department look upon reconstruction projects mainly as a means of providing employment. Of course if that attitude is taken it means delay, a continued loss of wealth, and a permanent loss in the form of dried-out- crops and soil erosion. During the spring in western Canada there is a very heavy run-off of water that may be urgently needed a month from now. A great deal of that water could have been saved if larger scale projects had been undertaken. Of course there is the other important point, that we are under a moral obligation to provide irrigation projects in the drought areas of the west, because those people were encouraged to settle in that area, in spite of the fact that the government of the day knew it wa9 not suitable for settlement.
I want now to make a few remarks and to ask a few questions in regard to the Red Deer river diversion scheme.

That comes under the
next item, too.

Then when we get to
that item I hope the minister will not say we can discuss only the St. Mary river project.

Last year we had an item of $10 million under the reconstruction department. This year we have an item of $5 million, and I understand that the minister hopes to get another $5 million. I think I shall have
to make a few remarks on this item, because I want to talk about more than just irrigation. I am sure a number of the fruit farmers and-others I represent, and all those in the Okanagan who were mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops, are somewhat disappointed at the delay in the plans of the government in connection with the application of P.F.R.A. to British Columbia. I support what was said by other hon. members
Supply-Agriculture

as to the great needs in the Cariboo and the Okanagan with regard to irrigation, but I just want to add a word or two about conditions as they exist in my own district of Kootenay West. We are not actually in the dry belt. We can grow crops without irrigation, but in some districts and on some land there would be a greatly increased yield with irrigation. I want to draw to the minister's attention the fact that in this district some thousands of acres are owned by the provincial government. There is one large tract consisting of several thousands of acres, formerly owned by the Christian community of universal brotherhood, which has been taken over by the provincial government from the mortgage companies, and which, I believe, could be developed very well under this scheme. The provincial government owns the land, and the provincial and federal governments could cooperate in developing it. Then the land could be sold to settlers. It is ideal for tree and small fruits. Then again there are thousands of acres of first-class bottom land alongside various rivers and lakes which can be reclaimed at very little expense. I know of one tract of some ten thousand acres in the Lardeau valley, first-class black loam, natural meadow, which can be reclaimed by lowering the bed of the river four or five feet, and this can be done at relatively small expense. The cost, however, would be too great for any small group of individuals to undertake. Then again we have a number of smaller areas along the Arrow, Slocan and Kootenay lakes that could be greatly helped by this type of legislation.
In these areas you would not be developing land that is marginal. You would be developing land which has a high productive value.
I think I am quite safe in saying there are probably fewer mortgages on the farms of my constituency than in any other constituency in the west. A mortgage there is quite a rare thing, which indicates productivity of the land and the skill and thrift of the farmers working it. However I am under the impression that this act might not be flexible enough to meet the varied conditions across Canada. I have spoken of these provincial lands, the dried-out land, and that which requires drainage, which I think should be developed jointly by the dominion and provincial governments. If the government is going to go ahead and assist these smaller areas which are already developed, something should also be done to assist the people I have mentioned, even if it is only to the extent of providing money at low interest rates, on long terms.
The people I represent are not people who ask for something for nothing. They built up 
that country as a result of their own labour. Possibly this act is not flexible enough to cover the varied conditions that exist across Canada. I throw out that suggestion to the minister, and I hope that at some time in the future he will take time to visit that district and see its potentialities. If he does I am sure he will be convinced that there are great possibilities for the application of this act in providing assistance to those farmers.

May I point out that no one has been discussing this vote. This vote applies only to the Palliser triangle and it is to build small dams and dug-outs as well as to provide community pastures and small irrigation projects. The discussion which has nowr taken place should have been on item 36, and all the other discussions should have been on item 31. Unless someone wants to discuss small dams and dug-outs and pastures provided for in this vote, perhaps it might be passed and we could get on to the proper vote.

Mention has been made of various areas in British Columbia which should be brought in under the P.F.R.A. and I was wondering if the
Creston area is one of those?

The Creston area is not in. None of British Columbia comes under the act for which this item provides money.
Mr. HARIvNESS: I will make the minister happy by staying strictly on this item. A thing I have had in mind for a long time is how the dividing line is drawn between the P.F.R.A. and the P.F.A.A. It seems to me that those two acts are working against each other, at least in the southern part of Saskatchewan and in Alberta. To illustrate, you may have a piece of land which is under P.F.R.A. and where people are being paid not to grow crops, to get off the land and go into certain valleys. Then you have another piece of land right next to the first piece where the people are being paid under P.F.A.A. to put in crops which may not grow. It seems to me that one of the great fallacies in these two acts is in an area such as southern Alberta where people will be paid under P.F.R.A. to leave certain areas and gather themselves into a valley, or leave altogether and go somewhere else so that the land may be taken out of cultivation, and in the same area another group of people are paid to stay there and put in crops which they probably will never harvest. They are given so much per acre planted. The thing I want to get is how the-dividing line is drawn or how it is decided which area is under P.F.R.A. and which is under P.F.A.A.

Supply-Agriculture

The only area under P.F.R.A. is the Palliser triangle, the dividing line of which runs through the city which my hon. friend represents. It extends northward to Lloydminster and then from Lloyd-minster almost in a straight line across to the Manitoba boundary at the northern end of the Assiniboine basin, then down along the east side of the Assiniboine basin to the Red river. All the area south of that is under P.F.R.A. The hon. member asked as to how the dividing line was drawn between the two.
I do not need a description of the Palliser triangle.

The P.F.A.A. may cover part of that area, or it may go up into the northern country. People are taken from submarginal land and put on good land or land on which water can be placed. That would be done under P.F.R.A. We encourage people to go into valleys which can be irrigated or on to land to which water can be supplied. Under P.F.R.A. we encourage people to get off sub-marginal land. All that is done under the one act. We pay the expenses of moving off the sub-marginal land on to the better land. For example, at Brooks we had 25,000 acres that were irrigated. We moved people off sub-marginal land in different parts of the Palliser triangle on to those 25,000 acres which had been irrigated. All but two of the families so moved are well satisfied and we have had complaints from only one of them.
When we move people off sub-marginal land that land is turned into a community pasture. These pastures run from 40,000 acres up to 115.000 acres. It is fenced in with a permanent fence, as near as you can make a fence permanent with creosoted posts and four barbed wires. The farmers who are left there are given an opportunity to use the pasture by paying fees.
It is correct to say that through P.F.R.A. we do encourage farmers to leave submarginal lands in order that they may be fenced in as community pastures. Once that is done, the farmers around the pasture are organized into grazing associations. We first take those in the first mile round about the pasture. Then we take those in the second mile, and we continue until such time as we have a sufficient number of farmers with sufficient stock to utilize two-thirds of the grazing capacity of the pasture. They then pa}- fees in order to put their live stock in, and the costs of operating the pasture are paid out of those fees.
When once those pastures are formed the sub-marginal land is taken out from under the P.F.A.A. There is nothing paid on those sub-83166-273
marginal lands. The only places where payments are made are on lands roundabout the pastures. The same principle applies all the way through the application of the legislation. For example, we say that a person who has had assistance in the form of irrigation cannot receive payments under the P.F.A.A. We have assisted him by putting water on his land; therefore he does not get assistance under the P.F.A.A.
That is just what I am getting at. You say that all the people surrounding the community pasture are taken out from P.F.A.A. except those who still happen to be staying there?

After the pasture is out from under P.F.A.A., the people who are utilizing the land roundabout do not draw on the acreage in the pasture; they draw only on the acreage they themselves are cultivating.

What the minister has said is quite correct, but it seems to me that the P.F.R.A. is the act which, if anything, will reclaim a lot of these dried-out areas in the west. I am all in favour of it and I believe it should be extended. However, one of the things in the way of its extension is the fact that sub-marginal lands are being maintained in cultivation or semi-cultivation under P.F.A.A. There is a conflict between the two acts and I wanted to get a reasonable explanation, which I do not think the minister has given.
Is there an extension this year of the area in which dugouts are being constructed?

There is no extension of the area except that there may be a municipality here or there where it is shown we have not drawn the line in the right place in order to take in the entire basin of some particular river.
To what extent are community pastures being extended this year? If they are being extended, where are you moving the people who are in those areas?

There is one in Manitoba. The only work that is being undertaken up to the present in Saskatchewan is the extending of pastures already formed. Areas are being added to them, and they are being added only because people have gone off the land. There may be one or two persons there, but mostly they would be on the edge of the area that is being taken into the pasture.

There are no large movements?
No.

Marketing service-
26. Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, and grants, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $777,599.	[DOT]

There are three cold storages in Winnipeg toward which we have made payments. The act provides that where we are satisfied, after inspection, that the cold storage is required and that all the conditions are met, we can pay thirty per cent of the cost of building the cold storage. That applies of course, to any organization, cooperative or otherwise, which is making cold storage available to the public. The Winnipeg plants are handled the same as the others. The only reason the payments are higher is that the costs of the plants are higher in Winnipeg than they would be in the smaller communities. The last agreement I think was made two years ago. Thirty per cent of the cost is paid, half of it the first year and the other half is divided over the next four years.
As to the small lockers, the provision in the act has been in the past that not more than fifteen per cent of any plant could be utilized for putting in small lockers. There was a reason for that under the conditions which prevailed before. These plants were practically all in cities and towns and were put in for the purpose that cold storage is usually put in for, to take in products from the public and store them and charge for storage. It was thought wise to limit the locker space to fifteen per cent, but that limitation is now being removed so that, where a group of people have got together for the purpose of putting in these lockers in the smaller communities, payment can be made on the same basis as for the larger plants. That is an entirely new provision. I do not think any payment has actually been made under it. The regulation has been changed within the last month or six weeks.
Will that be retroactive?

We have not considered that up to the moment. There are a number of these plants, but most of them we know of are put in by individuals who are simply hiring out the lockers. It is not intended that under the new regulation payments shall be made on those. There are reasons why that would be objectionable. But it is possible for a group of farmers or a group of village people or farmers to get together and organize one of these plants to serve the community, and then the payments can be made.
In the smaller country towns where the farmers get together and build themselves a plant consisting of small lockers entirely, they can still get the thirty per cent?
That is right.
Would that apply where a cooperative is already in operation, say a cooperative store, and the cooperative store decides to expand and build a cooperative locker in connection with the store?
That is a cooperative in the sense referred to here, but my hon. friend is aware that some organizations known as cooperatives are more or less joint stock companies.
I am speaking of a true cooperative.
Yes, where it is a true cooperative.

I know the minister is anxious to have this project completed. Everybody is wondering why the delay in this project. Will the minister say whether it is government policy to hold this project over as a measure to help solve our employment a few years hence? Would that be the reason for the delay?

No; the irrigation work is not bound up in that class at all. The irrigation work is not among those projects put on the shelf, so to speak. Irrigation projects are intended to be development projects which should be carried on whether we require relief or not; but it will be affected to this extent, that it is more difficult to get labour and material in times when work is plentiful than in times when work is not plentiful, and there might be some delay if the greater part of our labour was fully employed at something else. I am very glad to see this item of $1,500,000 for this project. This is to provide for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories, and there is a reduction of $300,000 for the coming year. My observation would be that within ten or fifteen years we may be able to do away with this item altogether. The hon. member for Lanark the other night mentioned the fact that there were twenty fewer cheese factories in eastern Ontario than there were the year before. In western Ontario it may not be quite as bad as that, but what is happening up there? If this trend of events continues for another ten or fifteen years we shall have a few cheese factories left there, because what is happening in western Ontario is this. A * man improves his factory, gets it in first-class working shape, and one of the large concentrated evaporated milk plants comes along and buys that factory. That does not necessarily put the factory out of business as a cheese factory, because at certain times of the year, when there is a flush of milk, they do make cheese, but in the winter months when milk is short they take the milk for their concentrated milk plants. Therefore the minister would do well to see what can be done
to encourage the production of cheese. I am not blaming him for this condition. I am not blaming the government, nor am I blaming those men who get an opportunity to sell factories and make a good profit; and I cannot blame the manufacturers of concentrated milk for buying a factory. But it is a condition that will certainly put the cheese factories out of business, in western Ontario at least, in the not too distant future.

I should like to ask the minister how this $300,000 reduction comes about. Has the minister definitely made up his mind that production of cheese will be so much less this year that he will not require the $300,000? I notice that $250,000 of the $300,000 is taken off the premium to be paid on quality cheese. There is no doubt that this premium on quality cheese has done much to increase the quality of cheese in this country, and I should think the minister ought not to make reductions at this particular time. Last night he endeavoured to tell us that cheese production in Ontario and Quebec was a month behind that of other years. If that should be the case, there may be a considerable increase in the production of cheese within the next few months, and it may be necessary that this amount of money should then be in the estimates in order that subsidies can be paid on this quality cheese. The other $50,000 is taken off the improvement of cheese factories, and I should like to ask the minister why there is the reduction of $50,000 in that regard.

The amount of decrease is $50,000 on construction subsidies and $250,000 on the premiums. The reason is partly as suggested, that there is anticipated a reduction in cheese production. There was a reduction last year. When we put through the vote of $2 million a year ago we were anticipating a larger production than we actually had, but it was estimated when these estimates were prepared that there would be some further reduction. That partly takes care of it. It does not make any difference whether there is or is not. If claims are made and amounts are due, under the legislation we must find the money. This is only an estimate of what we think will be required, and if more is required we shall require to have a supplementary next year to cover it. It will have to be paid whether it is in this vote or not, because the legislation provides for it.

35. To provide for administrative expenses, Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1941, $69,000.

This item has to do with
the Agricultural Prices Support Act. In 1945, at the dominion provincial production conference it was requested, I believe, that there be a certain acreage of potatoes in New Brunswick. The amount was 68,700 acres. The farmers planted 68,700 acres of potatoes and had an excellent crop. As a matter of fact, it was so good that they could not find a market for it. The agricultural prices board, I believe, guaranteed the farmers in New Brunswick that if they would sell their potatoes to the starch factories they would get a price of $1.65 a barrel. I understand that is correct. In the constituency of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield), who is away on account of illness, and who is interested in this matter, there were two starch factories, and the day after the prices board agreed to pay this price one of the starch factories was burned, with the result that the farmers could sell only a small quantity of surplus potatoes to another factory at Grand Falls, New Brunswick. The minister's department has received petitions from the potato producers of that section asking that, in view of the fact that this starch factory was burned, the board adjust prices to the potato producers so that they receive the $1.65 which was guaranteed by the starch factory if the potatoes were sold to them.
My question to the minister is this:	Is
any provision being made to pay the difference between the price that the potato farmers received and the amount that was guaranteed bv the starch factory? The amount paid for potatoes diverted to processing plants under P.C. 4295 was as follows: In New Brunswick, quantity, 241,764^ barrels. The amount paid is $120,837. I think I should give these figures

in hundredweights because I have not the second one in barrels. In New Brunswick, 198,763 hundredweight-

May I suggest to the minister that he might save time. I have not asked for the amount that was paid. He just mentioned an amount there which was small. 400,000	barrels to the starch factory is only a drop in the bucket. What I asked the minister was this. I thought the minister

The answer to that is that the matter was considered and it was decided that there was not any obligation, under the circumstances, to make further payment; and that if payment were made on the basis on which it was asked for, it would require the consideration of payment, not only there, but right across Canada for the same purpose.
The other part of the answer is that eventually the potato crop was all sold at a much higher price than anyone expected it to be at the time this agreement was entered into; that is, having the whole crop under consideration, a much higher return was received than was expected. Part of that was done through negotiating a contract with Britain to take 70,000 tons from Prince Edward Island which, by the way, was more than delivered; and there is the further fact that, as is reported in the press today-I think it is editorial criticism-the Americans overdid the

job of destroying potatoes, and after they had done that, the potatoes of New Brunswick were sold at a much higher price than anyone expected they would be. As a matter of fact, at one time we were being urged to stop shipment of potatoes out of Canada in order to make it possible to keep down the price of potatoes. We did not take that action. The final position was that the potato crop of the maritimes was sold at a much higher level than anyone expected it to be.

That is not my understanding. As far as the United States disposal of their potatoes was concerned, there was a great waste. We know that, but the United States government paid their farmers $2.20. They had better make their claim; that is all they require to do.
There is no claim to be made; but I received a telegram-

I was not through, Mr. Chairman. The remarks I wish to make arise out of a statement the minister just made to the effect that all the potatoes aje marketed.
I was somewhat under that impression until I received a telegram on Friday-a copy of which was sent to the minister's secretary- from a member of the legislative assembly in Victoria county informing me that there were quite a few potatoes left. He was complaining that we were allowing United States potatoes to come into this country, with the result that this was bringing the price of our potatoes down. He asked me to make a recommendation along that line, and to try to prevent United States production from coming in, in order to enable our farmers on the Saint John river to market the remainder of their potatoes.
I have not the telegram with me-it is in my office-but the minister has a copy of it. I had to leave on Friday; I just came back. The answer I received was about something else altogether, informing me that the price was above the support price. I know it is above the support price. It has been since about April 20, when the United States started buying from us. Naturally prices went up above the support price from May 1. A great many of our potatoes have been marketed, but now I understand that the farmers on the Saint John river, at Grand Falls, are complaining that they still have fifty or 100 carloads; I do not remember the figure, but the minister has it. The difficulty they are having in marketing at the present time, as represented to me, is this. Potatoes were coming in from the United States; and that has bothered our farmers on the Saint John river and prevented them from marketing their potatoes at a fair price. Has the minister any further information on this point?

Over the week-end they have sold fifty carloads from there to the United States. I presume they are selling them at United States prices, which are quite high. That is the reason we do not get them at $1. The agreement made months ago-last fall, as a matter of fact-was that the government would take at that price any potatoes which were left at May 1. My understanding is that there were no potatoes offering at that price on May 1, which must mean that there is a market for them somewhere at a higher price than that. Of course there are potatoes coming in from the United Staten now, and they are new potatoes. I presume the potatoes we had
