in the diningroom today on the sixth floor were new potatoes from the United States.
They were not very good.
Those potatoes are selling at a price two or three times as much as old potatoes are selling for in Canada.
Then I should like to ask if there are any old potatoes coming into Canada from the United States at this time.
I understand not; but there are old Canadian potatoes going to the United States.

I wish to ask the minister a question or two in regard to the board that was set up. In 1944, when the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed^ as reported at page 5576 of Hansard for July 29, 1944, the minister said:
... I make the suggestion to the house that we should content ourselves for the time being with the appointment of a permanent chairman and take two officials of the department and make them pro tem members of the board.
Our intention is that the board shall immediately begin to study the relationship of the conditions which now exist to the prices which now exist and that all facts with regard to matters of that kind be made available for use immediately the war is over. If I am the minister at that time it is my intention to appoint two permanent members of the board to act with the chairman when the operative part of section No. 9 is brought into effect.
Based on that statement, I want to ask what, recommendations or reports were made by the temporary board, and whether those reports are available. Various agricultural organizations have been interested in trying to find out just what work was done by that temporary board and what reports were made.
I should also like to know what members have been appointed to the permanent board, and if that permanent board is making further reports.

An annual report was tabled last session and another this session, both of which are available to hon. members. The two new appointees are Mr. Proulx, who is a farmer in Quebec, who at one time was an employee of the Quebec government and was also employed at one time on temporary work by this government; and Mr. Earl Kitchen, a farmer of Woodstock, Ontario, who was secretary of the dairy association before his appointment. They will be making reports annually, as the other board did.
Then there is an advisory board.
Yes, there is an advisory board of seventeen members.
Were any other reports made in addition to the annual reports?

Reports are made every time delegations come to see us. When a delegation comes to discuss dairy products we get a report from the board as to the situation. When they come to discuss meat products, or any other products, we get reports from the board to indicate what are the conditions.
Are those public reports, or are they private within the department?

I would doubt very much if they are public. They are the sort of things that pass from officials to a member of the government, advising as to what the position ought to be in relation to certain things. As a rule they are not made public.
Does the board give support to any other product than potatoes?

There was another point I wanted to bring out in connection with this item, in connection with the bonus paid for potatoes processed into starch. There was a great deal of criticism in my part of the country, particularly along the Saint John river, in regard to the date set for the guaranteed price, which was May 1. I brought up this point during the budget debate. I do not know what the next crop has in store for us, but if it should be necessary to take some action in the fall I should like to impress upon the minister, that while the action taken in regard to the bonus on processed potatoes seems to be quite satisfactory, the other part of the order in council, having to do with the board undertaking to buy as of May 1, fixes the date too late. There has been criticism by the farmers of my section of the country that when officials of the department went along the Saint John river they interviewed just a few big shots and the ordinary men could not get near them. How this diate of May 1 was arrived at, I do not know.
It was suggested by the delegation which came here from your area.
I was with that delegation, though I was not there all the time.
That recommendation came from them last fall, the first time they were here.

I cannot think they were in their proper spirits, then, to make such a suggestion. It is altogether ridiculous. Early in the year, in January, and possibly before that they began making representations to the effect that it was too late.

Supply-Agriculture
Experience showed it to be early?

I would not agree to that. As I say, because of the mistakes made by the United States government our potatoes went up in price, and the government did not have to purchase them after May 1. It was just a little short of miraculous. I again emphasize that if next year it should become necessary to do such purchasing, May 1 is much too late. This year, of course, we had snow until June and1 we have had rain ever since. But in ordinary years we start farming around May 1, and when we start farming the farmers do not have time to market their potatoes.
I am still waiting for an answer to my question. Did you support anything but potatoes?

No; potatoes were the only item that required to be supported. All the others were supported under the agreements made with Britain, and the floors have been maintained at higher levels than investigation would have shown it necessary to maintain.

Then would you tell the committee how you set a floor price? What knowledge do you go on, or whom do you consult? How do you go about it; because I know you are going to need to support a lot of things before many years. If you could give us an idea of how you go about it I can tell my constituents when they ask me.

What we do is negotiate a contract with Great Britain, under which we get the highest price possible. Then we calculate whether that contract price bears the relationship we indicated should be maintained as compared with the last three years of the war. So far, all those prices have more than taken care of what we undertook to take care of.
That is hardly right. You had not negotiated a contract with Great Britain-

I do not like the way in which my hon. friend, after asking a question, keeps telling me that what I have said is not right. Last night it was not true; tonight it is not right. I do not know what the difference is, but my statement is right.
You will admit that you did not negotiate a contract with Great Britain on potatoes.
I am not talking about potatoes. The hon. member was asking about other products.
He asked about potatoes, too, and that was the answer you gave. We have not a contract with Great Britain for all these things.
In the case of potatoes we took the recommendation of the committee that came here representing the potato people, as I said before.

Item agreed to.
Special-
S6. To reclaim and to prevent the flooding of valuable agricultural lands in the valley of the Lillooet river, near Pemberton, B.C., $100,000.
I have one or two questions to ask the minister, and also something to say about this item.
Eleven o'clock.
If you want to go on it is all right with me. I want some information concerning this item.
I think we can clean it up in a few minutes.

This is an item of $100,000 to reclaim and to prevent the flooding of valuable agricultural land in the valley of the Lillooet river. I am wondering why the dominion government has gone in there. I notice that project No. 1 covers 2,604 acres,
2,000	acres of which are Indian lands. My information is that the Indian branch recommended that money should not be spent in there. A little while ago the hon. member for Fraser Valley asked that something be done to prevent erosion and washing away of the banks of the Fraser river, but he did not get very much support. We have to go back to our people and tell them why the dominion government are going to spend nearly half a million dollars in connection with land which some of us think is not worth very much. Project No. 1 will cost $131 per acre and some of us are wondering who asked for this to be done. Is the provincial government putting up any money? Are the farmers putting up any money? I have been through this district, and if the dominion government is to come into our province to do this kind of thing I can point out more valuable land where the farmers have had to carry the load for many years. I want to ask some more questions on this item.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
